title: PUBLIC HEARINGS

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing on a request to appeal the Brevard County Zoning official’s April 22, 2026, interpretation regarding the applicability of Brevard County Policy BCC-100, Live Local Act, to subject property, Tax Account 2412106.
Billy Prasad, Planning and Development Director, stated this is an appeal of Brevard County Zoning official’s April 22, 2026, interpretation regarding the applicability of Brevard County Policy BCC-100, the Live Local Act, and the Brevard County Zoning Code to the property owned by Merritt Bidco, Tax Account 2412106, located in District 2.
Kim Rezanka stated she is in attendance on behalf of Merritt Bidco SPV, LLC; if she were in court she would be saying, "May I please the court" because that is what they hear; this is an appeal; the Board is looking at what is in front of it; this is not really in her opinion, a public hearing, it is a public meeting; she asserted that argument with the County Attorney and they are still working through that; this is somewhat of a new process; and it has not been done very often in Brevard County. She went on to say this appeal is seeking a Policy decision from this Board; this required the Board, not staff, to interpret its land development regulations and apply the County Code to the Live Local Act, Section 125.0557; she knows Commissioner Altman was in the legislature when this was adopted and that he knows legislative intent very well; however, the Bill’s sponsor called Live Local Act, a transformational market-driven consolidation of policies that provides attainable housing options for Floridians; Florida is tackling the complex issue from all angles by incentivizing private sector investment with historic State funding and common sense reduction in regulations; Merritt Bidco submitted the Live Local proposal to the Planning Department on April 7, 2022; the Zoning Manager opined that the 11.24-acre property did not meet the requirements; and in this appeal of the staff interpretation, the Board is evaluating the Planning Manager’s executive decision and it is making an executive decision, a Policy decision, here today. She continued on to say this is not a rezoning for a specific piece of property, they have already gone through that; this is an analysis of how the County will apply the Live Local Act; it is a Countywide Policy issue; the Board is not to consider infrastructure, roads, flooding, or even the Comprehensive Plan Administrative Policies; this is not an appeal of the denial of the rezoning; Florida Constitutional Article 5, Section 21, indicates that staff is not entitled to deference; it is no surprise that the staff report for this Item supports the Planning Manager’s opinion; but she asked should staff be grading its own paper. She inquired why there is no legal analysis or any review of the definitions from the County’s Code, from the Florida Statutes, or the Live Local Act; she mentioned the Board must look at the actual uses, the allowable uses in the AU zoning and not merely the zoning classification; the focus of the Live Local Act is the uses allowed, not the zoning classification; every parcel of land in Brevard County has zoning classification designation and that designation defines what uses are allowed; Florida Statute 479.011 defines allowable uses as the intended uses identified in the land development regulations authorized within a zoning category without requirement to obtain a variance or waiver; and the term includes conditional uses. She stated the plain language of the Live Local Act does not address in any way the name of a zoning classification; the act inquires an inquiry into the specific allowable uses; as shown in the County’s Code, page three of the packet…She asked if Commissioner Goodson could see this.
Commissioner Goodson responded affirmatively.
Ms. Rezanka stated the use of all land shall continue to be controlled and restricted by the provisions of the zoning classification designated for such land on the zoning maps; again, this refers to uses not the zoning classifications; the Planning Manager’s opinion focused solely on the property’s Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and discounted the uses allowed in the AU zoning category; but the CUP is dispositive of this appeal; the Merritt Bidco property qualifies under the Live Local Act for administrative approval of the multifamily residential because the property is currently zoned for commercial use; that commercial use is a hospital and a medical clinic; the CUP already exists and it was not approved by waiver or variance; the CUP was approved by zoning action in 1983; and the action approved additional uses subject to specific restrictions and conditions, a subcategory or permitted uses as defined in Section 62-1102. She went on saying that the CUP was not included in the appeal, it was included by reference; it is a 100-page document, here is page one, and it is in the packet; pages four, five, six, and seven also included in the Board’s packet shows the conditional use, what it was intended to do; further, the zoning official admitted at Planning and Zoning (P&Z) that a hospital could be built on the property without further zoning approval; moreover the County Attorney’s Office in an email dated December 3, 2025 acknowledged that a 1983 CUP such as this one, was only subject to revocation; and this CUP has never been revoked, in fact the Board of County Commissioner’s in 2003 refused to remove the conditional use on this property for a clinic and hospital use. She noted that is page 10 through 14; again, this is referenced in the appeal and incorporated by reference from the County records; the wishful phrases in the staff report of abandoned and nonconforming do not change the fact that a hospital or medical clinic can be built on this property today; the abandoned and non-conforming terms are unsupported conclusions that contradict the clear intent of the Live Local Act to allow affordable housing in areas zoned for commercial use; the other grounds cited in the appeal is that this is an area zoned for commercial and mixed use in the AU zoning; if one is unconvinced that the CUP allows the hospital or commercial uses, no matter what the intent of the AU zoning classification, even the staff report admits, several individual uses within the AU zoning classification may be characterized as commercial in nature, including fish camps, landscaping, businesses, resort dwellings, veterinarians hospitals, and farmer’s markets; and the staff reported attempts to paint the AU zoning classification as having a particular character, but the Live Local Act does not reference character of a zoning classification. She went on to say the Live Local Act does not care about character or the intent of the zoning classification, its only criteria is that the property is an area zoned for commercial, industrial, or mixed use; the State Legislature does not care what the County’s zoning regulations say; Live Local Act was adopted because of local government’s reluctance to approve new multi-family developments when local representatives are confronted with substantial neighborhood opposition; staff’s continued assertions regarding AU zoning classifications intent and how staff has always interpreted Live Local Act is not including commercial uses associated with AG uses as commercial uses is irrelevant; their assertions are irrelevant because State legislature did define commercial uses and mixed uses in 2025; the staff report completely fails to look at those definitions; and in fact, the statement zoning classifications are defined by their overall purpose and character, rather than by existence of individual uses within the classification does not make sense when looking at the definitions in the Live Local Act. She continued on saying the staff report indicates that House Bill (HB) 1839, the 2026 Live Local Amendment that excludes farm and farm operations from the definition of commercial use, supports its statements; this proposal and appeal were filed before that amendment and may not even apply in this situation; if it does apply, it does not exclude dude ranches, plant nurseries, private golf courses, fish camps, landscaping businesses, or numerous other conditional uses, which by Florida Statute conditional uses are allowable uses; staff attempts to disregard these commercial uses by stating these uses are associated with commercial uses or do not represent the principal purpose of the AU zoning classification; and again, the Board has to look at what it is zoned for, the uses allowed in the zoning classification, not the character or the intent of an ordinance. She added there is no factual support for these statements; Live Local does not care about the principal purpose of zoning classification; she recognizes that the Live Local Act is still evolving and not fully litigated; on page 15 it shows the definition of commercial uses which is in the Board’s appeal packet, which is in the Live Local statute; page 15 states commercial uses means activities associated with sale, rental, or distribution of products, services, and terms include but are not limited to retail sales, wholesale sales, rentals of equipment, goods or products, offices, restaurants, public lodging, food vendors, sports arenas, theaters, and for-profit business activities; and the highlighted items are what have been discussed in the AU zoning classification, 62-1334. She mentioned there are numerous, she believes eight in the appeal; on page 19 of the packet is plant nurseries; plant nurseries are a full-service retail sales and it talks about uses; a plant nursery is definitely a commercial use allowed in AU zoning; Live Local is still evolving, but the phrase zoned for is crystal clear; the County is stuck with the current AU zoning classification and its commercial uses as written; the solution is to amend the AU zoning code to take out commercial uses, not to contort the plain language of the AU zoning classification and the Live Local Act definitions; the Florida Legislature passed the Live Local Act to address the State’s housing crisis to deliver much needed affordable housing to communities in a timely manner; and it was also enacted to cut through self-interest and bureaucratic obstacles. She stated on behalf of Merritt Bidco SPV LLC, she respectfully requests that the Board reject and reverse the April 22, 2026, zoning official’s interpretation on one or both of the grounds cited in the appeal. She noted she will reserve her two and one-half minutes.
Chair Altman pointed out the applicant was given 15 minutes and he would like to set aside 15 minutes for staff’s comments if they need it, and then three minutes per speaker.
Mr. Prasad stated he does agree with Ms. Rezanka on one procedural point and that is that this application should be limited to the legal issues, staff’s interpretation of the zoning Code and applying it to State statute; that is really all that is relevant to this hearing; he would break what he heard Ms. Rezanka as saying into two distinct arguments; one is that the AU zoning class itself, is what qualifies this property under the Live Local Act; the second argument he heard was the CUP that applies to this particular property is what qualifies the property for the Live Local Act; and he will take them one at a time. He noted the first argument he would point to what the Live Local Act actually says; he read verbatim from 125.01055, "A county must authorize multifamily and mixed-use residential as allowable uses in any area zoned for commercial, industrial, or mixed-use and in portions of any flexible zoning area such as Planned Unit Development (PUD) permitted for commercial, industrial, or mixed use on property owned by a County, municipality, or school district, and on property that has more than three acres in size and owned by a religious institution.” And then it goes on from there; as Ms. Rezanka pointed out, the key is whether AU property makes this zoned for commercial use; attached to the Agenda is parts of the Brevard County Zoning Code and in that, one will see that AU is not within a commercial or industrial classification; in fact, it is in a single-family residential zoning classification; specifically, it is one of the least dense zoning classifications there is in the residential; it has a minimum lot size of two and one-half acres; when one thinks about what the legislature was probably trying to do with the Live Local Act, whether one agrees or disagrees with it, he thinks it is pretty clear what they were trying to do; if something was zoned for commercial, those intense commercial uses, it must make sense for multifamily or affordable housing to go in there; when that intent is taken and applied to the County’s Zoning Code and one looks at what the County has for AU zoning, he asked if that is really zoned for commercial uses; he commented staff contends that it is not; and that it is clearly meant to be single-family residential character with some agricultural type uses. He went on to say Ms. Rezanka pointed out that there was some language amended, but it did not come into effect until recently, in July, that made clear that farm and farm-related use were not commercial; that was always staff’s interpretation; he thinks that was the predominant interpretation by most people that looked at the Live Local Act; what the legislature did was clarify it and left no doubt about that; when one looks at agricultural land across the State, he does not think that was the intent of the legislature to convert that to a commercial classification; and they just made clear that was the case. He went on to say he will now move on to the argument about the CUP; the CUP is not zoned for that use; it is not a use by right, the Board has to specifically look at the specific characteristics of that property and determine that it is appropriate to do on that property; he would not say that it is zoned for that use; in this case it does not really matter because it was taken out of the AU Code; when one looks at AU he or she will not find clinics and hospitals under conditional use; it was removed after the CUP was granted; and the County’s Code very clearly indicates what that means is that it is a nonconforming use. He advised a non-conforming use is not part of its zoning; that is exactly what that means, one is nonconforming to the Zoning Code; if it is nonconforming to the Zoning Code that cannot possibly be what makes this zoned for commercial use; that is the fundamental part of the argument; and he will take any questions about any other part.
Chair Altman stated he agrees with Mr. Prasad’s interpretation of legislative intent; he was there so he has a unique perspective and he can tell the Board in no way, shape, or form was this intent to allow multifamily or affordable housing in the AG classifications; he can only imagine what would happen; agriculture is so important to this State right now, not only for food production but for preservation and recharge, water quality, and green space; it is critical; and he inquired what would happen if indeed there was a ruling that AU would qualify for multifamily zoning. He mentioned there is another negative impact that he worries about; if one has a piece of property that has General Use (GU) or maybe single-family use and one wants to go into production and get an agricultural zoning; if it was known then that someone could do multifamily, it could have an incredible negative impact on the County’s ability to zone areas to become agriculturally productive; and he does worry about it having a very draconian effect on the County’s ability to allow land owners to get a zoning because of the impact of that intensive use.
Mr. Prasad stated he agrees with him; when looking at the County’s zoning classifications today, the applications for rezoning, part of the staff’s comments include when there is a rezoning to commercial or industrial, the Live Local component of what the Board is approving could lead to that; if staff had to include that on every AU zoned property that is seen all the time in their zoning agendas, that would add an entirely different element when talking about a single-family residential classification with the minimum lot size of two and one-half acres to now thinking about 30 units per acre; that is what Live Local Act would apply in Brevard County; it is a drastic difference; and it is something the Board would have to consider.
Leon Kindred stated he is a resident of Merritt Island, specifically Sykes Cove which is immediately adjacent to the area being discussed; he was at the last long Board meeting in his red shirt and here he is again; he heard the comments today, and he is here to ask the Board to protect the integrity of the local land use laws and reject this appeal; the developers entire argument rests on a claim that a CUP from 1983 somehow transforms this agricultural land into a commercial zone under the Live Local Act; as has been stated a permit is not a zoning classification; the underlying zoning on this property is strictly agricultural and has been for decades; the Live Local Act is very clear, it only applies to land explicitly zoned for commercial, industrial, and mixed use; and furthermore, State law requires that commercial use be allowed by right without need for special waivers. He continued to say under County Code, conditional uses are never allowed by right; they require strict administrative oversight and can be denied based on community impact; he asked the Board to not allow a developer to twist an old, unexercised medical permit into a blank check to bypass the zoning maps; and please uphold the zoning managers correct interpretation and deny this appeal.
Robert Wise stated he would like to make a few comments that are irrelevant but he wants the Board to think about them anyway; he is representing not only himself, but the East Merritt Island Community Association (EMICA); EMICA discussed this project last March and they are unanimously against it; he realizes this is West Merritt Island, but all of EMICA’s members have to drive on Courtenay from time to time and they were all against it; he would like to remind the Board that when this project was first reviewed by the Merritt Island Redevelopment Association (MIRA) they were strongly against it and disapproved it; the Planning and Zoning Board considered it twice and had a split decision; but there was a solid half against it. He added he voted against it both time; and the Commission itself rejected the proposal back in April. He went on to say he cannot speak to the legal issues, but he hopes that the Board will find an interpretation that prevents this project from going forward.
Brandon Shannon stated he was here at the last meeting to speak in front of the Board and he is here again to reiterate his urge for the Board to deny this proposal for the project and to deny the appeal for this project; the developer’s argument rests entirely on a dangerous legal fiction, claiming that because an existing business operates on this property under the CUP, the entire 11-acre tract should suddenly be treated as commercial use triggering the Live Local Act bypass; zoning law is explicit, however, a CUP changes how land can be used, it does not change how the land is inherently zoned; the underlying zoning of this property remains AU no matter how many times a developer tries to rephrase it; a CUP does not magically erase AU zoning or strip this Commission of its local authority; because a property is fundamentally residential agricultural, it is exempt from the Live Local Acts commercial bypass provisions; this Commission already listened to the community and voted unanimously on May 7, to protect this neighborhood from high density overdevelopment; and the developers are now trying to use a loophole that does not exist to circumnavigate the Board’s vote, bypass public scrutiny, and override the infrastructure constraints. He continued by saying a CUP is a restriction, not a backdoor invitation for a massive high density complex project as presented today; and he would ask the Board to stand by its previous unanimous decision upholding the integrity of the Brevard County zoning laws, and to deny this appeal.
Diana Schommer stated she uses Pioneer Road frequently; she too hopes the Board will uphold its last vote of no for this development; Merritt Island does not have the infrastructure or the roads; there has already been an approval for 500 units up by the Kennedy Space Center; there is already 300 units going in on Fortenberry; there is a limit, this is an island, as to what the island can take; she would think that the infrastructure should precede any more of these developments; the fact is that the Live Local Act, the developer does not have to pay impact fees, sewer connections, or water connections; and she asked who is that all going to fall on because they do not have to pay for it. She noted it is going to fall onto the taxpayers; the County has already saddled the community with 800 units; this community does not need any more units; everyone can see that their taxes are going to go up for sewage improvements to handle all of this; it is going to have to go up for roads because the traffic is at its limits now; she also wants to say in the Live Local Act, it said that it does not have to rezone AU land, it is not compelled to do it like it is for some other zonings; she asked that the Board please honor that; and not to back track on this.
Pamela Steele stated she is a redshirt, she just forgot to wear it this morning; she lives in Sykes Cove which her access is on Pioneer Road; she spoke at the previous meeting when the Board denied the zoning; speaking here is not easy for many of them, but the precedence that this case sets is too dangerous for any of them to stay silent; if this room is not filled to the brim like it was last time, it is only because those residents are at work today and unable to attend, it does not mean that they are not listening online and still very concerned with the outcome of this meeting; make no mistake, they are watching and listening closely to this; and they are hoping this Board will do the right thing today for the residents. She went on to say she believes the Board denied this rezoning request based on public safety and health; she does not believe that the legislature ever intended to ignore public safety and health concerns in a local community with this Live Local Act; if the Board approves this appeal today, it is effectively telling every developer in Florida that the local zoning maps do not matter; the developer admits this specific 11-acre tract has sat completely vacant over 40 years, allowing them to exhume a dormant, long-abandoned administrative permit from 1983 to force State-mandated high density housing onto agricultural land; it is terrifying; if this argument succeeds, it creates a playbook that any developer will be able to buy cheap agricultural or rural land anywhere in Brevard County, find an old administrative permit in the archives, and strip the elected officials, who speak for the people, of their power to say no; the people elected them to protect the communities, environments, and their quality of life; she thinks the people have done a good job already at bringing the matters of flooding and traffic issues to the Board’s concern; this will significantly affect people’s quality of life, their environment, and nothing has changed in that matter; and she just hopes today that the Board holds the line, stands by it’s staff’s decision, and rejects this appeal.
Sarah Hodge stated she would like to thank the Board for denying this at the last meeting; she expressed her appreciation to staff for the information because it is so correct; she mentioned the people appreciate it and feel they are cared about and that the Board wants to help them; the County knows this is not a good program, it is not a good thing for this community; she would ask that this be denied; and she supports any speaker that wants it denied and anyone else who speaks today because they are much better speakers than she is.
Tom Reedy stated he is there to express his strong objection to the proposed Rangewater Merritt Bidco apartment project on Pioneer and Courtenay; the people all know, they have talked about the roads, the infrastructure; he had a whole speech but everybody has already hit on it; all the people are asking the Board to do is to please stand by its original decision and protect the community from this project that obviously does not fit, does not serve the residents, and does not improve the area; and he would urge the Board to reject this appeal.
Valerie Reedy stated she is here because of the decision before the Board today does not just affect one neighborhood, it affects every community in Brevard County; the people are there because Merritt Bidco, the entity associated with Rangewater Real Estate, is attempting to use the Live Local Act to bypass the County‘s previous denial of their rezoning request for a 222-unit high-density luxury apartment complex at Pioneer Road and North Courtenay Parkway; the community followed the process, they showed up, they provided evidence, and the rezoning was denied; now, the developer is trying to overturn that decision by using a loophole that was never intended for this purpose; their argument is simple, but deeply flawed; and they claim that because a medical office operates on an agricultural residential land under a CUP, the entire property should be treated as commercial, but the permit is not zoning. She explained a CUP allows one specific use, it does not change the underlying zoning category; if this Commission accepts the idea that a CUP can magically transform AU land into commercial land, then it is not just approving one project, it is rewriting zoning interpretation for the entire County; that means any property with a special permit could suddenly be treated as commercial land under the Live Local Act; that would allow high-density apartment complexes to be built anywhere with no public input and no community review; the Live Local Act’s purpose is to support workforce housing on a property that is already zoned commercial; it was never intended to treat conditional uses as commercial zoning or to bypass the public’s role in local land use decisions; its intent is to add housing where it fits, not to redefine zoning categories; and this is about more than one development, it is about protecting the integrity of the zoning in Brevard County and ensuring that the CUPs remain what they were intended to be, limited exceptions, not zoning changes. She added it is about preserving the public’s rights to participate in decisions that shape the communities. She asked the Board to uphold its original zoning denial and reject this attempt to bypass local zoning through a loophole, doing so protects not just Merritt Island, but every neighborhood in Brevard County.
Ms. Rezanka stated she does not know what the intent of the AU Zoning Code was when it was adopted; she does know it contains commercial uses; she does recognize the unintended consequences of the Policy decision the Board could make today; the reality is, the Brevard County Zoning Code allows conditional uses; there is a conditional use on this property; in fact, the conditional use has already been used on this 14 acres, which she thinks is why this was never revoked; as she stated 62-1253, the adoption of zoning classification, the use of land is controlled by the zoning classification; the zoning classification does not have an intent per se, it has uses that are allowed; the Live Local Act says must authorize multifamily in an area zoned for commercial or mixed-use; and because the AU allows agriculture and commercial uses, it essentially is a mixed use, but it definitely does allow commercial uses. She mentioned she does understand the unintended consequences; she does not think the legislature actually thought this would ever happen either; many Zoning Codes do not even have an agricultural zoning classification, they have a use table; the problem is the AU zoning classification, not the Live Local Act; this is clearly zoned for commercial; and this is not a rezoning request, Live Local does not require a rezoning request, it is simply to allow multifamily affordable housing in areas without requiring a rezoning. She went on to say whether it is an AG zoning classification or a General Use (GU) classification, which she has not looked at the GU, it may have the same problem, she does not know, but the problem is with the County’s Zoning Code and the solution is to change the County’s Zoning Code; with that, she believes this clearly meets the definition of commercial uses in the Live Local Act, and it also meets the definitions of mixed-use; this is a CUP that has never been revoked, that was declined to be removed by the Board of County Commissioners at one point; the County’s own Zoning Manager has said that a hospital could be built on this vacant spot today; and she would ask the Board to reverse the appeal.
Chair Altman noted he has a quick question; and when she said that the CUP in this site has been used, he inquired what it was used for.
Ms. Rezanka replied it is used for medical office buildings; she explained it is on the four acres that are not for this project; it was all a 15-acre CUP; and part of the CUP has been exercised.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation to Ms. Rezanka.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, asked if the Board would like to hear from him.
Chair Altman responded affirmatively.

action_text:
Chair Altman stated under good suggestion, he would like to move Item H.5., to the end of the Agenda, it is a big Item and people probably do not want to wait around; he advised it is the adoption of the proposed FY 2026/2027 ad valorem millage; and he reiterated that will be heard last.
Chair Altman called for a public hearing on an ordinance to sunset the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District at the end of 2029, while honoring any existing contractual obligations and commitments of the District.
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, stated this is the public hearing for the ordinance to sunset the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District at the end of 2029.
Richard Heffelfinger stated his only question with this is there were some concerns about this water district previously on another Agenda Item; he pulled up the Agreement and he realized this does not happen until 2029; they will pay off their bonds, he thinks he understands that correctly, and the County is going to take over that because that water treatment plant is basically finished and will not meet the new requirements for water; his concern was in the ordinance it makes some language, Brevard County shall honor those contractual obligations and commitments to the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District that exist at the time of its dissolution; there is this period between now when the Board says it is going to dissolve this and 2029; it also says, “shall transfer the title of all property owned at the time” and he asked if that time is in 2029 or is that now; it says, “the County shall assume all indebtedness,” he assumes he thinks the plan was they are going to be out of debt with the bonds by 2029 and then the County will take it over because the place is probably not real good; and he inquired what happens between now and then and if they have the authority to go into indebtedness between now and then. He went on to say his question is the County told them it is going to take this away, they are currently collecting fees, people are paying for water and sewer, some people came forward to say they do not like their rates, but all he can say about that is who sets their rates; he commented he assumes the rates are high enough that they are paying for the current running of that facility; he asked between now, 2026 and 2029, what happens; he mentioned he does not know what the state of that facility is, other than it is implied that it is not real good because it is 50 years old, and it does not meet the current requirements; if it has a major malfunction between now and then, he asked who pays for that and would it potentially put that Special District in a bad spot; is the County going to inherit a flaming bag of poo if something bad happens; is staff planning for what could potentially happen between now and then, so it knows what it is getting; and he stated it concerns him that the language says the County is going to assume their indebtedness. He commented it would be nice to know what it is anticipated to be; he asked if this could be delayed, as the Board is making a statement right now saying it is going to accept this, and there is a lot of time between now and then; why not just take the responsibility at the time that they run out of that bond; and he noted that is his only concern. He commented he does not know if anyone can answer those questions and if any knows what that facility could potentially do to the County in the period between now and then.
Chair Altman asked if Mr. Fontanin wanted to answer quickly or wait until the end.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, commented he thinks that is a legal question; from the first sentence in the staff report, the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer Utility District is a Dependent Special District governed by the Board of County Commissioners with the Brevard County Utility Services Department responsible for District service operations; it is this Board that is going to decide what the District does in the next several years; this Board sets the rates, there is an Item later on the Agenda where the Board was going to consider… actually the rates come back next meeting, but the Board will be addressing the rates and the District very soon; that is all well within the purview of the Board of County Commissioners; and the Board should not be surprised by anything the District does in the remaining time.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated he appreciates that answer because he was just concerned that it sounds like the Special District was just something set up to allow them to take bonds; he asked if that is correct; and he continued by saying if there is not a problem and the Board does not think there is a problem, then he no longer thinks there is.
Sydne James asked the Board to take a pause and not move this Agenda Item forward at this time; she stated in 1999, County Commissioners here voted to buy the Barefoot Bay facility and to keep it a Special District; one Commissioner at the time noted that Barefoot Bay customers were paying more but used roughly half the amount of water of the average utility customer in unincorporated Brevard County; she said this is unfair, the unfairness has not only continued, it has increased immensely; in 2022, Barefoot Bay rates increased 10 percent; this was followed by 13 percent increases for the next three years; as she said two weeks ago, Barefoot Bay customers are the only residents in unincorporated Brevard County who shoulder the burden of maintaining their own wastewater treatment plant; and all the other plants share the cost burden among all the other customers. She went on to say this is unfair and unjust, and unaffordable to many Barefoot Bay customers; Commissioner Adkinson asked about dissolving the Barefoot Bay Special District and incorporating them into the Countywide system now rather than wait until December 31, 2029; the County Attorney essentially said it is impossible because the $4 million still owed for the purchase of the system must be paid for by the users of the system; this was the end of the discussion, but it should not have been the end, their rates have increased 49 percent over four years; and they will remain high even after the rollback of the 2026 increases. She inquired what the 49 percent increase was for; she noted it was not for paying off the bonds; their rates were already on schedule to pay off the bonds at the end of 2029; those increases were for coming into compliance with Florida Statutes, repair and maintenance of the facility, and funding to construct the new facility; the Board members all agreed the new facility will not be a special district; finally, Barefoot Bay customers will no longer be treated as the black sheep of the County; they are full citizens of the Brevard County; and she asked the Board to please stop treating them as second class citizens now, rather than waiting three and one-half more years, it is never the wrong time to do the right thing. She added the Board has several options to right this wrong, one would be to dissolve the District now and have the residents continue paying off those bonds. She stated the resulting increase to Countywide customers would be negligible, but the savings to Barefoot Bay customers would be profound; and there are other options, please take time to research and consider other options so this can be fixed now and not wait three and one-half more years.
John Requa stated in the meeting on July 7, 2026, the County’s legal counsel kept referring to Barefoot Bay as a Special District, however, he noticed on his property tax that after paying his amenities for the year, he pays Brevard County taxes to the tune of over $2,100, even with homestead; he pays for SJRWMD, imagine that; they pay for water for other places; they pay school tax, roads, repairs, and all the other taxes; just the water and sewer plant, how convenient that is that former Commissioner John Tobia in 2022, as far as everyone is concerned in Barefoot Bay, he threw them all under the bus; he agreed for increases on Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer Plant, in addition to the money on the bond and that was to make improvements that were already promised; and he does not know if those improvements have ever been made. He mentioned the Commissioners and the trustees back in 1999 made some very bad decisions that has brought all of this to where it is today; the people are pleading with the Board to correct it; that is all they want; in addition to this, since he was here last time, he received a call from Utility Services Department telling him that they had watched him on video and that they would get the answers to the four questions that he sent Mr. Fontanin by certified mail; they said he did not receive it but it did arrive at the mail room because he got a receipt around midnight; he has not received a response to that; and he believes if he had a response to those four questions that it would show where there has been a waste in funds for the improvements of the water and sewer facility at Barefoot Bay; and to answer this man’s question over here, they are a deed restricted community with a Board of Trustees, and Barefoot Bay does not own the water and sewer facility. He went on to say Mr. Fontanin can tell people that; it has been taken over by Brevard County and they intend to replace it by 2029, with a new facility; they do not know what that is going to cost them or what the rates are going to be; he personally finds that suspicious; the County is not going to put in a multi-million dollar plant and not have any idea what it is going to charge the consumer; and he asked Mr. Fontanin that question two years ago and he said he did not know. He stated he knows there is an answer to that question; the people would love to know what that is; the people are pleading with the Board, they are hurting; himself, he can afford to pay the water bill, he just received a $163 water bill for one month, he can afford to pay it, but there are many that cannot; like he said before, with the water, the problem with homeowners insurance on modular homes and taxes, it is going to turn Barefoot Bay into a trailer park; it is going to fall; that water plant not only supplies Barefoot Bay, it is Crystal Bay, Sebastian Lakes, and Snug Harbor; it is more than just this community that water plant funds; and he pleads with this Board to do the right thing, the Board knows what the people want.
Chair Altman advised those are all the cards; he will bring it back to the Board; and he inquired if staff has anything they wanted to add or respond to before discussion.
Mr. Fontanin responded by saying no, sir.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she will make a motion to hold a public hearing to adopt the ordinance to sunset the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District.
Chair Altman stated there a motion to adopt an ordinance; this would not be the final decision, this is only to set the public hearing; and he asked for a second.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will second the motion.
Chair Altman asked what the date is of that ordinance.
Mr. Fontanin stated he believes in the ordinance it is December 31, 2029.
Chair Altman clarified the date of the actual public hearing.
Mr. Fontanin advised this is the public hearing.
Attorney Richardson asked if Chair Altman is asking for the public hearing on the rate resolution.
Chair Altman stated the public hearing on the motion for this ordinance; and asked that Commissioner Adkinson repeat that motion again.
Commissioner Adkinson stated her motion is to adopt the ordinance to sunset Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District.
Chair Altman stated he wants to make it clear this is for the adopting the ordinance to sunset.
Commissioner Feltner stated he will second that.
The Board conducted the public hearing and there being no further comments or objections it adopted Ordinance No. 26-10, repealing Chapter 98, Article VI, "Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District," Sections 98-181 through 98-200, of the Code of Ordinances of Brevard County, Florida; dissolving the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, a Dependent Special District of Brevard County, as of December 31, 2029, pursuant to Section 189.071, Florida Statutes; providing for the continuation and administration of existing contractual obligations of the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District; providing for the disposition of district-owned property within Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District; repealing all Ordinances inconsistent with this Ordinance; providing for conflicts; providing for severability; providing for repeal of Code Sections and effect on Code; and providing for an effective date.
attachments: Business Impact Estimate Statement for Barefoot Bay Sunset Ordinance.pdf
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Ordinance to sunset the Barefoot Bay Water & Sewer District at the end of 2029, while honoring any existing contractual obligations and commitments of the District.

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing on approval of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan for the Brevard County HOME Investment Partnerships Program Consortium.
Juanita Jackson, Housing and Human Services Director, stated this is the public hearing for FY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan for Brevard County HOME and Community Development and Block Grant (CDBG) Programs; they are estimated to receive $1.3 million in CDBG funding, $1 million in HOME funds, and Brevard County will receive about $447,000 of the $1 million, and member cities will receive the remaining $623,000; as a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) consortium, Brevard County as a lead agency is required to submit and annual action plan for how HOME and CDBG dollars will be spent; public input was sought through a 30-day public comment period with advertisements in Florida TODAY, Ebony News, on the County website, and social media; staff requests approval of the FY 2026-2027 annual action plan for the Chair to sign the required certifications, assurances, and applications for Federal assistance for CDBG and HOME to HUD; and for the County Manager to sign Program Grant Agreements and authorize housing staff to complete the proposed actions and projects.
There being no comments or objections, the Board approved the Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan; authorized the Chair to execute the required certifications, assurances, and the Applications for Federal Assistance for the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME grants; authorized the County Manager to sign the CDBG Program and HOME Program Grant Agreements and Disbursement Agreements with the four Brevard HOME Consortium member cities upon approval from HUD; authorized Housing and Human Services, as contract administrators, to use competitive procurement to secure contractors to complete proposed activities and projects and to endorse agreements, amendments, and modifications for activities and projects identified in the Action Plan and procured by Housing and Human Services, after approval from Risk Management and the County Attorney’s Office; and authorized the County Manager to execute any necessary Budget Change Amendments (BCRs).
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Final Public Hearing and Approval of the Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan for the Brevard County HOME Investment Partnerships Program Consortium

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing to adopt the proposed FY 2026-2027 Ad valorem Millages.
Keith Neterer, Budget Office Director, stated this Item requests that the Board set the proposed Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 millages; the millages approved under this Item will be the millages that appear on the Truth in Millage (TRIM) notices mailed to the taxpayers in August; the list of millages to be levied by the County is attached to this Agenda Item and were used for budget development; Florida Statutes requires that by August 4, the taxing authority must inform the Property Appraiser of upcoming millage and meeting information for use on the TRIM notices; and that notice will serve as announcement for the first public hearing that will be held on September 8, with the second and final public hearing to be held on September 22, 2026. He continued to say all operating millage rates have been established within the Brevard County Charter Cap limitations and the voter approved millages have been set within the restrictions of the voter approved maximums.
Richard Heffelfinger stated it is great to see that things are not busting the cap; he is shocked because he went to budget hearings or budget workshops that he thought people were going to die this year; he does not know why that did not happen because he believes the Board, along with the County Manager, talked about what was needed to be done this year to solve some of those budget workshop problems; he saw nothing but problems; he did not see any specific budget asks, he saw problems; if he has this right, the County is going to advertise that it is not busting the cap; but that is not the end of it, the Board still has to have deliberations, talk about budget, and it could very easily on this dais decide that it is going to bust the cap on this; he asked if that is correct; he noted he understands that could happen, it will not, but the issue still exists; and they have identified with that impact study thing, a huge deficit and where they are going to pay for stuff. He advised he heard concern from the Board of what is was going to take to overcome some of these projects; that six-story building comes to mind; the water, maybe he is messing that up because that is some kind of fund that is different, it does not take real estate tax for that; he heard concern on infrastructure and yet he sees no bust in the cap; he is not upset, but he does not know where the County is going to get the money for all that other stuff; and Commissioner Pritchett said maybe the Board could consider a gas tax, but he thinks that was already talked about. He inquired if that is the percent of gas tax to help for transportation because it was shot down, the Board does not want to pursue that; if the Board waits too long, it only gets worse; the Board either takes on the problem now and tries to address it; everyone knows what the problem is, the impact fee study did a wonderful job of documenting where the County is behind; it is seriously behind, $3.5 billion in transportation over the next 10 years; he thinks he read that number correctly; the Board better start doing something now, it only has 10 years and he does not know how the Board is going to do that; he would like to hear a plan; and he hopes that everybody considered what needs to be done with the millages, that this is accurate, the Board is not going to bust the cap, or that there is not going to be some major concerns later in this budget period where people freak out; everybody is good with this, he is good with it, and he hopes the Board is good with it; he does not know what it is going to be 10 years from now or the next couple of years; it is always try taking a bite out a time; the Board is not taking any bite out now; if there were really any emergencies, he would have expected a bite; and the Board would have a conversation about how to fund that. He asked if the State is magically going to step in and pay for all of the stuff; he commented he does not know, he is just trying to get some insight into this, he was scared; and he is still scared.
Chair Altman stated he would like to make a motion just to put this into posture so the Board can more forward, have debate, and then a vote; he thinks that would be helpful; and he asked if he may pass the gavel and move from the chair.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, replied affirmatively stating Chair Altman may move from the Chair.
Chair Altman passed the gavel.
Chair Altman stated he moves to set the General Fund millage rate at the supermajority rate of 3.0942 and have staff bring back a resolution setting forth the critical needs that were presented at the budget workshop in April; he would also ask that the staff bring back recommendations on allocating the additional $17 million with the focus being on public safety, infrastructure, and restoration of reductions that were necessary to balance the budget; he thinks this helps fund needed infrastructure and improvements; it is a measured action because it will still remain the lowest millage rate in the region; it will still be lower than the millage rate that was back in 2023, but it will allow the County to address some very simple, important, critical issues. He went on to say prior to August 4, the Board must set the millages that will be sent out on the TRIM notices; these millages can be lowered, but cannot be increased without setting additional notices at a cost of approximately $180,000; this takes a conservative approach, just not the final millage rate; there is still the ability to lower them but it cannot raise them; if the Board were to go with a lower rate it would box it in and put the County in a bad place without having the ability to hear from the public and deliberate; that is why he thinks this is important to this to give the Board the flexibility; to set the millages above the current limitations, the Board must adopt the resolution setting forth the funding of critical needs under the Charter; and a supermajority is required to adopt the resolution and millage rates above the Charter limitations. He noted staff will bring back this resolution at the tentative budget hearing on September 8, 2026; that still gives the Board time to evaluate; here are some of the issues that he thinks are critical, and this millage rate would allow the Board to address them; the animal shelter replacement is incredibly important to the community; the Brevard County Jail infrastructure, looking at what the Sheriff is up against in maintaining that jail facility, there is a serious threat to the ability to protect the public and house inmates in the County jail; the North Brevard Government Center (NBGC) and other facility repairs; he was in that facility a few months ago when raw sewage was raining down on the heads of the Property Appraiser; he cannot emphasize the dire straits that facility is in; and it is a $3 million replacement. He stated $5 million for animal shelter, $3.5 million for the Jail, $3 million for the NBGC, which is the County seat and an embarrassment that there is such disrepair; it does provide road surfacing of $1.6 million; provides the Tax Collector’s ability to implement the voter approved millages from the School Board; and it restores $2.4 million of critical reserve levels, which is an allocation of about $16.8 million. He went on to say he thinks it is a starting point; he would support this as a final, but he wants to emphasize that it at least gives the Board the ability to get with staff to have meaningful dialogue and give the public the opportunity to give testimony on these important needs; and that is his motion.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she will second for discussion; she is really relieved that Chair Altman did that, she was trying to figure out who she was going to talk into getting a second on that; she spent the weekend on this; she still needs a lot more time; she is looking at the statistics of where the Board was a few years ago; with Amendment 3, and she really thinks that is going to pass, it just looks like a good thing to a non-political person; she knows it is going to be painful trying to figure out how to get more tax dollars; in District 1, they are trying to get data together, but the storm water and drainage issues are huge right now; and she has to figure out how to get those things covered. She mentioned the Reserves are down to under 10 percent in the General Fund which has got her attention and needs to be fixed pretty quickly; the budget right now and going into next year after the Amendment 3 happens, the County has a certain percentage it is allowed to raise it; if the Board does not get this to a fairly decent level right now, which is not a whole lot if doing the 3.094; that is what will base next year off of; the State of Florida mandate about six years ago, had everyone’s income increase over six years; this is the last time doing that, but it has been a great obstacle trying to figure out how to get everybody with salaries paid Countywide; and all the businesses are suffering too. She continued by saying everybody our there is having a lot of struggles; the Board needs to figure out how to keep the County’s core services running; there are a couple things she would like to bring back to the Board for discussion, the Local Option Gas Tax (LOGT); that could be placed on the ballot with a three out of five vote, or vote it through with a supermajority; that would be something that even the tourist would help participate in; she is just looking for how much the County has to have with those items and figure out how to get there with the least amount of pain to the constituents and what they can afford; and she thinks that is a good start. She added she was hoping for that herself and she is trying to find some other ways to get some more funds in and she will completely support that today.
The Board approved the FY 2026-2027 proposed millages, to set the General Fund millage at the supermajority rate of 3.0942 for the purpose of notification to the taxpayers by the Brevard County Property Appraiser; directed staff to bring back a resolution setting forth the critical needs that were presented at the Budget Workshop in April; directed staff to bring back recommendations on allocating the additional $17 million, with the focus on public safety, infrastructure, and restoration of reductions that were necessary to balance the budget; and authorized the County Manager to complete the Florida Department of Revenue’s Certifications of Taxable Value, Forms DR-420.

action_text:
Katherine Wall, Central Services Director, stated this is a resolution authorizing a loan in a principal amount not to exceed $17 million from the Florida Local Government Finance Commission pursuant to its commercial paper program, to finance capital projects and land purchases under the County’s environmentally endangered lands; this is a request for the County Commission to approve a resolution authorizing the borrowing of an amount not to exceed $17 million in principal; authorize the Chairman to sign and execute the resolution and the various documents; and authorize the County Manager to implement the budget amendments that are necessary to implement this request.
Lewis Kontnik expressed his appreciation to the Board for what it has done here today and over the years; he stated the Board has balanced between growths, which everyone knows is necessary, so they are fortunate to be getting that in measure, and also the environment; the Board has certainly done that with Environmentally Endangered Lands (EELs) in the past, it has done it with the Lagoon, it is being looked at again for the Lagoon; and on this Item it seems like a yes please go ahead with it; the County has that money, it did a vote, it is changing the approach that it is realizing the money for expenditure; and he fully supports it. He reiterated his appreciation to the Board for its balance.
Vince Lamb welcomed back Commissioner Pritchett; he stated in 2022 he served as chair of the Political Action Committee advocating for the passage of the referendum that continues the EEL Program and also authorized up to $50 million in funds for conservation land purchases; this referendum passed with more than 70 percent of the voters choosing to tax themselves to continue the program and to place more land in conservation; two years later, this Board authorized $3 million in funds for conservation land purchases; the conservation fund organization was engaged to assist the program in finding and acquiring lands; properties have been acquired using these funds including Hundred Acre Hollows; and currently, 12 properties submitted by land owners have been determined to meet the requirements of the program by the Selection and Management Committee. He went on to say the total value of these properties is $80 million; the Board will have some choices to make in the future; each of these properties must be approved by the Board of County Commissioners; often the EEL Program can find matching funds from other sources, including the Water Management District; more than a year ago, this Board authorized $17 million in conservation land funding with specification that it was to be provided by bonds; County staff developed concerns about the use of bonds and determined that commercial loans were a better choice; this issue is back to the Board with just that small change; and he would certainly encourage the Board to pass it. He commented he is excited that the EEL Program, conservation land program, is up and running, and vibrant right now as these funds are needed to keep that going.
Chair Altman stated he knows this is implementation of public vote for EELs; it is also implementation of the action the Board took last year through the budget process; the only difference is that staff can probably do a better job than he explaining why the use of commercial paper rather than bond; and maybe staff should explain.
Ms. Wall explained currently, the commercial paper program right now is an all-in 3.26 percent where if the County got a bond it would be about 4.25 percent; and this is a better, more economical means to get the money for the EELs Program.
The Board approved and adopted Resolution No. 2026-061, authorizing the borrowing of an amount not-to-exceed $17 million in principal from Florida Local pursuant to the terms of the County’s existing Loan Agreement with Florida and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; authorized the Chair to execute the Resolution and various closing documents with respect to the issuance of the loan; and authorized the County Manager to approve all necessary budget amendments to appropriate funds to capital projects and land purchases under the County’s EEL’s Program.

body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: NEW BUSINESS

action_text:
Billy Prasad, Planning and Development Director, stated on February 25, 2025, the Board directed staff to begin the process of conducting an impact fee study pursuant to the Florida Impact Fee Act; through a competitive procurement process, Benesch was selected for consulting services and drafting the study; they have completed the study and a representative from Benesch is here to answer any technical questions regarding that; while the County conducted a study on impact fee rates in 2014, the Board at that time, chose to retain the current impact fee schedule adopted on October 30, 2001; and as such, the County’s current rates were established more than 25 years ago. He went on to say the Florida Impact Fee Act has been amended often over the years; some particularly relevant changes have occurred in each of the past two sessions; in 2025, a provision was added to state, “A local government may not increase an impact fee rate beyond the phase and limitations under this paragraph, if the local government has not increased the impact fee within the past five years”; those limitations effectively prevent the County from increasing impact fees more than 50 percent, which itself must be phased in over four years; subsequent to that, in the 2026 legislative session, the Act was amended further to add in additional methodology and technical requirements to the impact fee study among other amendments; and these amendments were effective July 1, 2026, and the supplement to the study attached to this Item addresses those requirements. He continued by saying given that, staff believes the study meets all requirements to justify amending impact fee rates, districts, and related regulations; the study indicates that nearly all impact fee rates are justified at far more than the 50 percent cap; because the County is statutorily limited to that increase, staff is proposing increases to the cap; and the couple of exceptions that would not be to that 50 percent limit are solid waste facilities and fees applying to what are considered industrial uses in the context of impact fees. He stated due to required changes in methodology and calculations, residential solid waste fees would see a decrease; on the flip side of that, because industrial uses have been exempt from impact fees since at least the 1990s, they have effectively not been adopted throughout the period of the study that the current fees are based on, therefore, the Board has the authority to establish those at those rates shown to be justifiable by the study, and include things like warehouses, mini-warehouses, and manufacturing; to be clear, what staff is seeking today regarding fees is only preliminary direction in drafting ordinances, no fees will be increased until the Board holds a public hearing after due notice on the ordinance amendments; if the Board ultimately does adopt new impact fee rates, those would only apply to new development, not existing structures; and in addition to fees, staff is seeking to amend the impact fee districts to allow maximum flexibility. He noted the study supports the concept that the residents and visitors are highly mobile; having five transportation districts, for example, unnecessarily hinders the County’s ability to direct funds where they are most needed and benefit the public the most; it also limits the ability of the developers to partner with the County in funding large transportation projects in exchange for impact fee credits that can be used throughout the District; in summary, staff is requesting the Board take the following actions today; one adopt the attached impact fee study; two, provide direction to staff to draft amendments to the impact fee rate schedules at the maximum impact fee rate justified through the study or as capped by Florida Statutes, whichever is lower, and amend impact fee district to provide maximum flexibility; three, issue legislative intent and permission to advertise amendments to Chapter 94, Article 4, Division 3, Impact Fees, and Chapter 62, Article 5, Impact Fees, of Brevard County Code of Ordinances; and four, any other direction of the Board. Mr. Prasad went on to say he wants to take a moment to address Mr. Heffelfinger’s question from earlier today on how the financial process works; each are segregated by impact fee type; library facilities, for example, are kept separate from transportation facilities, and they are held in an account and tracked over time; and some are carried forward, particularly transportation projects because they are very expensive, so they wait until there is enough funding for a certain project and once the advisory board recommends a project it is brought to the Board for disbursement on those projects, but until that time that the Board approves a particular allocation, the funds are held in their accounts.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated to add on to what Mr. Prasad just stated, if the Board looks at the adopted budget and the proposed budget, each impact fee has its own Section underneath Planning and Development; and it shows what is in it and what the revenue is.
Richard Heffelfinger stated he brought this forward because he is disappointed that the County had a study and paid a lot of money for it, but the study was not delivered early enough to take action before the State interceded with their regulation; he believes that is true; the study showed that Brevard is seriously behind on funding some major services; the impact fee, he thinks the study showed one of them was over 400 percent and needed to be increased; these are long-term planning things; he believes they were all looked at five to 10 years, and he knows transportation looked at a five percent deficit, a five-year deficit, and then an overall 10-year for planning purposes; and there are a list of roads. He noted it is wonderful insight into how the County assess what it needs to do based on these impacts; he assumes they are all impacts from new development; there was an opportunity, it would have been brutal though, he realizes there is a balance with impact fees, too much then no one wants to build here, it would be too expensive, and as the Chair identified it would possibly raise the cost of a house because they are going to pass that on to the home buyer, and he understands that; also one cannot say to not pay impact fees and let the residents pay it out of their own pockets; somewhere there has to be a balance; he feels really bad and it is unfortunate that the County did not take action earlier to try to get a little more than 50 percent because that 50 percent does not put a very big dent in it; and it is well documented. He mentioned he has not read the complete impact study; he is sure there is a lot of wonderful information and insight; the important thing was the impact fee study demonstrated needs; he pulled a quote out of that that says it all; it says with reduced impact fee levels, estimated revenues are not sufficient to fund projects needed for any of the service areas, under this option, the existing population will subsidize new growth or the level of service will degrade; people already know what is going to happen; he asked what is the plan since the County did not take any real action; he mentioned this thing decremented like four percent where it could have taken out as much as 38 percent of that projected cost; the County did not put a big dent in it, it put a little dent in it because it is limited by the law; he thinks staff is asking for the maximum amount that the State will allow; it is a four-year progression; the County will get some of it back, but it is very small; and he inquired what the County is going to do to get the rest back or as a citizen what should he anticipate because he thinks this is going to kill him. He added the millages is going to be talked about later; he asked again, what the plan is, what is in the transportation impact fee right now, and how much money does the County have; he commented he is a little disappointed and a lot concerned; and he thinks everybody in Brevard County should be.
Commissioner Feltner stated he thinks there is something to be corrected; and he asked Mr. Prasad if some date had been missed that impedes the County.
Mr. Prasad clarified by saying in the legislative session of 2025, July 1, 2025, is when the key language took effect, therefore, the County never had the opportunity to raise it more than it is being raised today, at least in the last couple years; to quote what was added in, in 2025, “A local government may not increase an impact fee beyond the phase and limitations under this paragraph if the local government has not increased the impact fee within the past five years”; the other operative language that was added this year, they do not even get to that because the County had not increased fees in the last five years; and therefore, they could never go beyond that 50 percent anyway.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation for the clarification.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she is fairly positive about approving this because she would like to see what the numbers look like; since that is all that this is doing, it is not setting the numbers right now, she would like to see what it looks like; she knows that people all say that they will end up having to pay the cost themselves, but maybe they do not need to, maybe they could have builders not pass all of it along; but for her, she would like to see what the numbers are.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she does not have a problem right now with adopting it; she needs a little more time to dig into the numbers; she had a real busy weekend with the budget; there might be some other things the Board can talk about as far as getting some more revenues in; she would like to have all these things as a topic one evening so the Board can have a discussion because she was looking through maybe a Local Option Gas Tax (LOGT); that might be a little easier for the constituents; she wants to get all the numbers from the County; she was looking at the public service tax, but thinks that would be really hard on residents because the electric bills seem to get quite high right now; and there are just some things that she wants to dig into if the Board would give her a little time on that before it sets any kind of direction to staff about how to implement it, would be her request today.
Chair Altman stated he thinks that is a reasonable request; and he requested clarification that the Board will not be setting them today.
Mr. Prasad responded affirmatively; he stated there is a minimum of a 90-day notice period; this would just be having staff do legislative intent to draft the ordinances; and again, there would be a 90-day notice required before it came back to the Board.
Commissioner Feltner asked if there is a point where the Board has to have final adoption; and if there is a time frame, it comes back later this fall, but has to be before the end of the year, is it something like that.
Mr. Prasad replied no, the Board has to adopt the study, but not necessarily act on the rates; the Board is adopting the study today, but that does not require it to act on that study; and once it has adopted the study, he believes it has four years to act on the study, or somewhere in that period.
Chair Altman stated he has historically been against the concept of raising impact fees; he is going to vote in favor of this and he wanted to say why; one, something is fundamentally different today than a few months ago and that is Amendment 3, that is going to have a significant impact on local government’s ability to provide needed improvements, infrastructure; he thinks the Board needs to keep every option open that it possibly can; also there has been a lot of effort in his District, significant developments and developers trying to get around the level of service impacts that staff is doing a really good job trying to enforce and maintain as much as possible for the County roads; thirdly, just the incredible feedback from his constituents; by far the single greatest complaint that he receives is the level of congestion and the amount of development; and he does not think they are anti-development, but the level of congestion on the roadways and how the County is going to address that has had a big impact on him.
The Board adopted the Impact Fee Update Study; provided direction to staff to draft amendments to the impact fee rate schedules at the maximum impact fee rate justified through the study or as capped by Florida Statute, whichever is lower, and amend impact fee districts to provide maximum flexibility; and issued legislative intent and permission to advertise amendments to Chapter 94, Article IV, Division 3, “Impact Fees,” and Chapter 62, Article V, “Impact Fees,” Brevard County Code of Ordinances, consistent with the Board’s direction.

Marc Bernath, Public Works Director, stated this is a contract for sale and purchase and addendum for fee simple parcel and utility easements from Wheeler Farms Incorporated for the wastewater treatment and water treatment facilities relocation project, southwest of Doty Drive on the north side of Micco Road in Palm Bay, District 3; the approach for the new treatment facilities is to have a dedicated access drive from Micco Road to the facility; and this would help to bring that project to fruition.
Richard Heffelfinger stated he brings this one forward because he thinks water is important; the County is asking for a dedicated drive and it says the reason it cannot use the current drive is that it is a dirt road and it is subject to flooding; this is the map and he thinks he understands it correctly, that is the plant and this is the dirt road that comes in currently for the plant access; he does not know what is brought in, maybe water that needs to be processed, he does not know he is just trying to figure out the logistics of why it needs another road; there is a dirt road that is subject to flooding; he does not know what the geography here is, but he doubts that this parcel of land that the County is trying to cut a road through or get an easement for is any lower or higher than that road that is over there, and that the County already has a utility easement for; he does not remember the cost, $700,000 or $900,000 or something, but the County is going to get an easement here and it is going to buy some of the property, get a utility here, and then put a road here, if he understands correctly; and that road is going to come in to support the new plant. He pointed out this parcel was bought for $5 million and he assumes that is part of the new plant; this parcel is already owned by the County and that will be part of the plant; this plant is going to be a big footprint here; this parcel right here that was already bought, used to be a trucking depot or storage facility; one can see this beautiful road that comes in with a big turnaround right here and a couple of buildings; it has an entryway that looks like it could be graded to do all kinds of transportation and it was supporting a trucking plant; it seems like it has gone dilapidated but he does not understand why the County needs to cut a road through here if it already has this road because it is just going to get the property and still have to pave that; and there is a big problem because they have to bridge a canal. He went on to say he does not have any estimates, he does not know if the County has done a cost study of should it use this, improve this, buy this and put in a road and bridge, or just use this road coming in from here; he does not have all the information he is just asking crazy questions because when he sees what is trying to be done here, he questions why; he assumes these properties are all going to be utilized for ponds and whatnot that is done with water for water processing; he reiterated there is road that comes in right now and inquired why the County needs to buy the property, build a bridge to cross the canal which is expensive, and is this truly less vulnerable than this dirt road that it already has, it is part of the parcel and all it has to do is pave it; and of course he imagines these people do not like the trucks driving past, but it happens. He asked if the Board could clarify that.
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, responded by saying just to go through a few items, the cul-de-sac road that is referenced that one can gain access from the north, that was from a previous plan development; quite honestly to get access through, one would have to go through Grant-Valkaria; Grant-Valkaria right now is not allowing access into that; they do not want the neighborhood traffic; there is going to be a 10 million gallon per day wastewater plant and a 10 million gallon per day, ultimate water plant; the amount of deliveries and trucks, 50-foot trucks, they cannot make that turning radius on Doty Drive; it is a dirt road, a recreational road, and he thinks it may be posted at 25, but he drives 20 because of the geometrics of it; and once getting into facilities of such, in addition, the billing office that is currently locate in Barefoot Bay is also going to be moved to this site. He noted the amount of traffic, not just day-to-day car traffic, but also the truck traffic, keeping in mind they also have to have an ingress egress construction, so when this is getting constructed there is going to be severely heavy equipment; and having an access dedicated for that provides a better logistic overall for the project.
Chair Altman commented that was a good explanation.
The Board approved and authorized the Chair to execute the Contract for Sale and Purchase and Addendum a fee simple parcel and utility easements from Wheeler Farms Incorporated for the wastewater treatment and water treatment facilities relocation project, southwest of Doty Drive on the north side of Micco Road in Palm Bay, District 3.
