title: Thad Altman, Commissioner District 5, Chair

action_text:
Chair Altman stated J.1. is a proposed donation of real property from Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to Brevard County for use by the Brevard County Utility Services Department to facilitate design and construction of a new advanced water and wastewater treatment facility.
Mr. Fontanin continued by saying what this is, is as the County is currently in the process of designing what staff being called South Brevard Water and Wastewater Treatment Plant, which is ultimately not only going to serve South Brevard within the Brevard County Utility Services area, but it is also going to be the replacement for the Barefoot Bay Water and Wastewater Treatment Plant; as staff is going through this, some of the design consists of the design being in Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District property; these projects are being funded on the Countywide system; there are occasions when staff fills out grant applications, they ask who owns the property; and the feedback staff was getting from some agencies were when they say it is a Brevard County project, but it is the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, it kind of gives like a sense that the County might not have the full entity of it, so given the fact that in three and one-half years that Barefoot Bay is going to sunset, and to give the County hopefully a better opportunity in achieving grant funds. He stated staff is asking the Board two things, and he guesses it is two parts; and he asked that the Board, as the Governing Board of the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to donate the property, and they are asking it as the Board of County Commissioners to accept it.
Hanna Welander stated she is a customer of the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District; she is addressing Agenda Item J.1., the proposed donation of real property from Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to Brevard County for use by the Brevard County Utility Services Department to facilitate design and construction of a new advanced water and wastewater facility; there are, as she can tell, four properties that are being proposed to donate for $10; the property facts sheet has an additional piece of property, which was not shown on any map that she could tell; and it is 30G-38-01-HJ-*-31, and its assessed value is $12 million. She continued by saying her investigation revealed that the value amount of the properties that were being asked to donate or that the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District is being proposed to donate is valued at $14,963,430; the original purchase price, which varies from 1974, 1985, 95, 96, the total of the purchase prices were $1,077,800; these figures were based on the 2025 property/real estate amounts today and were obtained from the Brevard County Property Appraiser website, so this is a huge amount of money that is going to be donated; meanwhile, Barefoot Bay and other impacted communities continue to pay for the existing plant and the land; and as the Board previously heard under F.7., since she is taking notes on her notes, and she asked the Board to bear with her, it is a mess. She mentioned since 2022, customers of Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District have been paying towards the nutrient plant, as they understand it, as well as the current one, which they still owe $4 million she believes; there was a 54 percent increase in their rates over the five-year period, which was addressed under Item F.7.; the land value alone, she believes, should offer the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District some relief; she asked how much customers of Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District paid currently towards the bond, the existing bond outstanding amount, their existing bond; and she expressed her appreciation to the Board for its time.
Sydne James commented she is flabbergasted, Mr. Fontanin just said that the new facility’s cost will be borne by the County because it will be, she assumes, because it is going to be part of the Countywide system; she wants to share some documents; she wishes she had the overhead, but she will hand these to the Commissioners after; this is from January 14, 2022, when the rates got raised by these double digits, it says one of the reasons why, in order to utilize the new facility for not only Barefoot Bay customers, but also unincorporated future development, the decision was made to locate the new facility outside of Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer boundaries; and this will make the new facility part of the Countywide system, so that has been in the plan at least since January 14, 2022, that this new facility would be in the Countywide system. She remarked it says the proposed rate adjustments of the 2025 through 2026, 35 percent would go to cover the rise in operating maintenance costs, while the majority, or remaining 65 percent of all of these increases, again 54 percent over five years, 65 percent of those increases will be associated with the need for capital reinvestment; the only capital reinvestment in this document is all the new facility; they have been paying 65 percent of their rate increases have been going towards paying for this new facility, which now the County is saying is not going to be in Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, it is going to be in this brand new thing; that means they have been paying, and they will be paying, on two at the same time; yet, he just said that the new facility is going to be borne by the County, the cost to build; and she asked why have they paid so much, how much have they paid. She stated May 9, 2024, audit, the department plans to build a water and wastewater system, new system, outside the Barefoot Bay District; the District will be decommissioned when this new system is completed in about five to six years from now; May 9, 2024, five to six years from now is before 2029 when it is supposed to be decommissioned, it is supposed to be built by them; it says once the new system is operational, all of their requirements will be provided by the new system; she is just confounded how the County can take the land from the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, which Ms. Welander just said, is almost a value of $15 million, transfer it, and then all of the money they have been paying to build a new system now is going to be borne by the County; and she asked if they get a refund.
Terry Brewer stated he is sure the Board has seen this, the map is of the proposed purchase properties in the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, which is outlined in blue, and the purchased properties are in red; as the Board has heard from the previous speakers, the valuation of that property has gone up by millions; it just seems inconceivable that elected representatives representing all of them in Brevard County Water and Sewer District, as well as the rest of the County, could look at this and say, “they paid for that, $10, oh, that is fair;” and he just cannot believe that. He went on to say it is inconceivable that they do not get credit for what they invested in to going towards what they are going to be paying in the future; he is sorry; and he asked the Board to think about it and sleep on it.
Chair Altman provided documentation from Ms. Brewer to the Clerk.
Commissioner Pritchett asked if she could ask a couple of questions because she has missed a bit of this; she inquired from listening to the comments, if the County is making them go to its system; she stated she thinks there was communication a long time ago when they were doing this, they had their own water system; she noted if they have this land, maybe the Board should not be doing this, and let them figure out how to build a plant since they have funds; and she does not know, she is just asking questions. She stated she thinks it was really good that Commissioner Adkinson did an audit making sure the County was not overcharging fees and getting it back; she has to study this a little more, it is a little bit different than what she remembers; she asked if the County is doing a disservice to them, or did they want to do this; and if the Board can give her a little background, that would be great.
Commissioner Adkinson noted she is going to let Mr. Fontanin answer that, as clearly, he has all of the numbers and the history about how this all happened, because technically it all happened before she got here.
Commissioner Pritchett pointed out she remembers a long time ago they had the bonds and she thinks the County bailed out some bond issues and helped with that; but she did not know if the County did something different here recently.
Commissioner Adkinson stated as she understands right now, the County has in this particular Agenda Item; the County is donating the land and them accepting the land; and she is going to let Mr. Fontanin explain.
Commissioner Pritchett asked for accepting the land, if it is for the County to build a water plant for these residents.
Mr. Fontanin explained the idea is there was an Agenda Item a month or two ago where, not Barefoot Bay, not a donation, but Brevard County purchased 80 acres off of Dottie Drive; the purchase price, he believes, was $5 million; that was done through County funds; the idea of this is the County is looking, first of all, the Barefoot Bay Water and Wastewater Plant fall under the jurisdiction of his Department as being a Brevard County Utility Services asset; the deciding factor of that is, the Board because it acts as the Governing Board of the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District; the idea of this is as staff is moving forward with the design; they could have done a bulk sewer/bulk water agreement between Barefoot Bay and the County, it chose not to; that way, the County was just going to blend them in with it and incur the cost of that through the Countywide system, given the fact that they are now going to be sunset; and the whole idea was to just clean up some of the design components of this. He asked can the County wait until 2030, and he remarked he supposes; but as the County received a Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) grant application, and they were asking who owned the land; it causes some confusion in Tallahassee when putting who the entity is and the land owner is not the same; and staff seeks this as an opportunity that the investments the County is going to be making at these facilities, that it could start implementing that to kind of get a running start.
Commissioner Pritchett asked if he knows what the estimated cost is going to be to get this plant rebuilt and up and running.
Mr. Fontanin replied right now the water and wastewater treatment plant, the County is looking tentatively now at about $150 million, but he would not be surprised if it goes higher; staff went out and solicited for a construction manager at risk, which means the County already has a contractor onboard; they are already giving the County early estimations, it is only about 15 to 20 percent in the design, it is still in permitting and whatnot; this is absolutely going to be $150 million dollars; the initial capacity is really the replacement of what Barefoot Bay has; there will be the option to add on capacity as development outside of the Barefoot Bay District grows; but this is really the investment on replacing the water and sewer capacity from their plant. He pointed out their plants do not meet FDEP regulations; they are not advanced wastewater treatment, which means their current wastewater plant exceeds the nutrient limits for effluent, the investment, due to the age of that; believe him, the County has put money in it over the 20 years to kind of revamp it; this latest of it now being advanced wastewater treatment, due to age and whatnot, the County made the decision that it needs to go new on the facility; on the water side, they are already at capacity essentially; and due to the Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) requirement, they do not have the technology at that water plant in order to do the PFAS removal. He stated the new water plant is going to be reverse osmosis, which is literally the cleanest the County can get water to be.
Commissioner Pritchett noted that is good; and she asked for $150 million, with the amount of customers on it, how long it is going to recoup the amount of money the County is spending building a new plant.
Mr. Fontanin responded from the Barefoot Bay Water . . .
Commissioner Pritchett stated yes.
Mr. Fontanin replied it is not . . .
Commissioner Pritchett stated maybe she can get it from him later, as that is an interesting question, because then all of the rate . . .
Mr. Fontanin advised it would be a long time . . .
Commissioner Pritchett stated payers are going to have to cover the new plant, too.
Mr. Fontanin stated because once staff looked at it, they are really looking at it as a getting melted in.
Commissioner Pritchett stated the County is going to need some more capacity up in the north area, too, so the Board knows in the future coming up, but that is expensive; and she expressed her appreciation to Mr. Fontanin.
Commissioner Adkinson asked if the Board has to make the motion as the Governing Board of Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer, and then the second motion has to be as the Board of County Commissioners.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, responded there will be two motions; the Board will wears its hats as the Governing Board of the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, and make a motion to donate the property; then it will change hats to the Board of County Commissioners and accept the property; just to be clear, regardless if the Board does this now, when the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District sunsets in 2029, by operation of Statute, all of its assets are going to come to the County anyway, so this is not anything sinister, it is accelerating it now for purposes of Mr. Fontanin and Utilities ability to make grant applications and start that money coming in now for the new plant.

action_text:
Chair Altman advised the Board has in a presentation the potential impact of the November property tax amendment on Brevard County.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated he just has a few slides that highlight a few items; the paper is attached to the Agenda for further reading for the audience and for the Commissioners what the County has on Amendment 3 on the ballot is; what the County is being asked to do is a vote to change the State Constitution and it has impacts on the obviously, on the County if the voters vote for it; what Amendment 3 will do will limit use of the County property tax, the ad valorem tax, which is the first line one sees on his or her tax bills; it would restrict those tax revenues can only fund the core services; and he is actually going to read them, they are on the slide. He went on to say the core services, if this is voted upon, it would be in the State Constitution; core services can only be spent on public safety, including law enforcement, fire services, and emergency medical services; core service would be education in public schools, which obviously is not the County, that would be the School Board infrastructure including construction and maintenance of roads and bridges, stormwater management, and other public infrastructure; including flood control, natural resources projects, bond obligations, pension obligations for local government employees; he is going to assume that is mostly for cities that have their own pensions; it, as the County, is under the Florida Retirement System (FRS); and then operation and administration of counties, municipalities, constitutional officers, and other authorized government functions. He commented in this County, when looking at that that would be the Board of County Commissioners, Tax Collector, Sheriff, Property Appraiser, Clerk of the Courts, the court system, and the Supervisor of Elections will all be included in the core services; some notes to remember is what this vote does is it lowers the Countywide taxable value by raising the homestead exemptions up to the first year to $150,000; the second year it is going to raise it up to $250,000; when he has the slide showing the impacts, he will be talking about the $250,000; this would only apply to homesteaded properties; for the non-homesteaded properties and commercials, there is an assessment valuation cap that they can go up to 10 percent in the current law; now their increased assessed value can only go up to five percent; and then the part he wants to make sure everybody knows, and it is right there on the bullet point, is just because a service is defined as a core service, that does not mean it is going to be held harmless. He pointed out that will include, and he will show the Board in just a minute, that includes law enforcement and Fire Rescue; the next slide shows a couple of the anticipated impacts from the second year when the homestead exemption goes up to the $250,000 note; the Parks and Recreation Department would face an $18 million loss; he is pointing them out because Parks and Recreation, number one, receives municipal service that the voters voted upon; they are going to lose about $7 million from the lower taxable value; and then, Parks and Recreation is not defined as a core service. He stated the property tax the County spends now, the ad valorem, it would not be able to use for Parks and Recreation; law enforcement, through their Multiple Services Taxing Unit (MSTU) will lose, for the audience, MSTU is Multiple Services Taxing Unit, they will lose about $7 million; the County’s Fire Rescue would lose about $6 million; the libraries are in about the $6 million range; he is rounding off the numbers; Mosquito Control will be impacted to a lesser extent, and the Environmentally Endangered Lands (EELs); some of the services that the County currently fund with its General Fund will be prohibited; and the County will not be able to use those ad valorem taxes. He mentioned right now the County has about a little over $2 million a year going to the Transit Services, that money would disappear, and they use that as their match; Housing and Human Services has somewhere in the neighborhood of $3.2 million; they use that for all of their different programs for match; that also includes the Veteran Services office, which is in Merritt Island, Palm Bay, and here at the Government Center; and that is not an eligible core service, so the County would have to find different ways to fund that. He asked looking at the green, if this happens, the voters approve, and what can the County do; he noted staff does not know the impacts yet and they are sitting down with the Board working it through; but he is going to use libraries because it is kind of a simpler explanation; libraries receive their tax bill; looking on the tax bill one sees the library tax right there; they are going to have an impact of somewhere in the $6 million range; staff will be coming to the Board if they libraries lose $6 million, with what they need to do; he asked if library branches closures need to be looked at, do they look at reduce service hours; and if there is a combination thereof. He pointed out by looking at the services hours, the County has to make sure it has the minimum staffing in a libraries, as just one employee cannot be working in a library; he or she has to be covered, and it has to be made sure the shifts are covered; it is not just a simple answer if 20 percent is lost, the hours are closed down by 20 percent of the branches; and staff is going to have to look through it and talk with the citizens. He stated with Parks and Recreation, that is a much bigger picture; there are over 100 parks throughout the County; the definition of Parks and Recreation is right there, the County provides parks and it provides recreations; he asked does the County look at cutting back on parks or cutting back on recreation; he advised the Department has already taken a look; he asked does the County raise the fees on the recreation; he inquired can the County raise the fees high enough to keep the programs going; by looking at youth leagues and similar things, could that be a large number; and he noted staff does not know that yet, but it can be a big number. He mentioned summer camps are important to a lot of working families; he forgets the number, but it is $175 a week or something like that; he asked if the County raises the fees so high to keep the summer camps going that people cannot afford to go to summer camps; how does the County find money to help fund those; last, but not least with Parks and Recreation are the boat ramps, it has a very active boat ramp program; he does not know what to call it; the County provides it up and down the County; and most of the public boat ramps are County-operated. He asked what the Board does for boat ramps, so there are some very important things to look at; and staff does not even know the details. He explained talking about law enforcement, fire rescue, mosquito control, he wanted to point those out because, libraries is kind of a simpler budget to work with because they are self-contained; but then, seeing the impacts on Parks and Recreation, it is pretty obvious what the Board is going to see some of the impacts to Parks and Recreation. He stated the next slide is in the report; this shows the gap between core service expenses and the general ad valorem; looking at the blue line, that is the core services; it includes Public Safety, Sheriff’s office, Road and Bridge Facilities, and Constitutional offices; there are actually some General Fund that goes to Natural Resources on their Code Enforcement side; then when looking at the burnt orange line, that is the County’s general ad valorem tax revenue; based on trends, they expect the trends to go up on the blue line; that burnt orange color is actually data coming back; County staff works with the Property Appraiser; they have been good at giving it some data; and that is following the next two years. He stated assuming there will be a bit of an increase, he is going to read this straight from the report, because he wanted to point out this gap, there is already have the existing gap, whether this passes or not; currently, in this Fiscal Year, the gap between General Fund revenues available for core government services and the cost for providing these services is covered by a substantial portion of other major General Fund revenue, which includes the one-half cent sales tax, State-shared revenue, Florida Power and Light (FPL) franchise fees, communication service tax, and other miscellaneous revenue; as the gap between property tax revenues and core services expenditures continue to widen, an increasing share of these other major General Fund revenues must be redirected to support core government functions, leaving fewer resources available to fund County programs and services that would not be eligible for property tax funding under proposed amendment; the County’s issue here is it is already having a gap, so it would be very difficult for the Board to say it will take all of the State one-half cent sales tax and direct it to Parks and Recreation; it is basically not available because the County is using those funds to fill in that gap which the Board has now; and as the Board can see, the gap is getting wider, so it may have to look at core services facing some sort of reduction. He went on to say if the Board wants to keep Parks and Recreation whole or Transit, it is going to have to look at different funding sources because it is going to use the alternative funding sources to fix that gap; he just wanted to point that out; and the County has core services, so it can only spend the ad valorem in the core services, then it is using other revenues to make sure it balances that budget, which limits its ability to fund the other departments that are not core service departments.
Chair Altman asked if the actual effect of the amendment basically says if it is not a part of these core services, that no ad valorem can be spent on it, or is it limited; and what the actual impact of that is.
Mr. Liesenfelt replied the County cannot spend the ad valorem funds if it is not a core service.
Chair Altman asked if the County has to find some other user fee or whatever.
Mr. Liesenfelt responded affirmatively
Chair Altman commented he knows 93 percent of the County’s parks are for playgrounds, children; 76 percent run summer youth programs; 86 percent for team sports; and this is an anti-children proposal, or the County just charges user fees.
Mr. Liesenfelt advised as the County does the user fees . . .
Chair Altman interjected by saying or the County does away with these children’s programs.
Mr. Liesenfelt noted the County is not to the point yet, but he could see the Board having the discussion if it wants parks that have playgrounds and swing sets and nothing else, or does it want recreation programs and not have standalone parks that do not offer anything besides recreation programs; he added, also in the parks the County runs a number of community centers; he actually had the conversation with the supervisor; the County’s community centers are wonderful early voting locations, they are perfect for them; another interesting thing is the community centers, the way the County does evacuations for hurricanes, the community centers are the number one evacuation centers right now; and they are designed to do that, designed to help, so staff works . . . so he means there are some impacts beyond just parks in those situations that affects how the County provides service, and how it affects people’s services.
Chair Altman stated just to clarify, the County is not allowed to use ad valorem on the core services.
Mr. Liesenfelt mentioned outside the core services, the County is not allowed to use ad valorem.
Chair Altman inquired because he thinks having some of the basic understanding as the County Manager presents, how public safety is defined, he means mosquitos and mosquito outbreaks, infectious diseases; he stated he would think the core of what the County is doing to protect public safety in Florida is Mosquito Control; but as he understands, Mosquito Control is not included; and he asked if the Legislature fixed that problem.
Mr. Liesenfelt advised no, he will be straight on honest, staff had a meeting with all of the counties, county administrators, and Florida Association of Counties online, and staff asked that question about Mosquito Control and MSTU; he forgets the exact chart of accounts, but it does not include Mosquito Control under public safety; at that moment, the definition of Mosquito Control is not a core service; maybe if this passes and the implementation they might add it in, he does not know; but based on the chart of accounts and how the State budget basically allocates the revenue, it is not a public safety function.
Commissioner Adkinson asked when Mr. Liesenfelt is talking about core services being law enforcement and fire, on one hand he is saying the County is going to make sure that it funds them, and on the other hand, he is saying the County is not holding them harmless, what it actually looks like when talking about reducing law enforcement, and say fire at the moment, those two things.
Mr. Liesenfelt replied he does not have the budgets in front of him, but it is the Sheriff’s Department, if the County cannot fund a different way . . . let him back up, the Sheriff’s Department may face a $7 million cut based on the MSTU; at the County’s Fire Rescue Department, talking red and blue, it is on the fire operations side, it would face a $6 million cut; there is a way the millage could be raised on the non-homesteaded properties to bring back that revenue up to that point; but 35, 40, it would be like a 35 or 40 percent increase to the millage rates.
Commissioner Adkinson asked when he says for the fire, is it the operations side . . .
Mr. Liesenfelt interjected by saying that would be equipment . . .
Commissioner Adkinson asked what he is talking about.
Mr. Liesenfelt advised the big red trucks, he uses technical terms, not the ambulances, yes.
Commissioner Adkinson inquired if that is maintenance, is that getting new things, is it replacing old . . .
Mr. Liesenfelt interjected by saying it is everything.
Commissioner Pritchett asked if that means the Board would have to close an assessment to cover those services.
Mr. Liesenfelt replied he guesses the Board could raise the . . . the Board has to do this for the assessment; a study has to be done to show the assessments are based on how it benefits the property/household; he is not going to get the term exactly right; if this passes November 3rd, the Board cannot come in November 4th and say it is going to raise the assessment by the equivalent of that $7 million, it has to do a study and go through the process; and it is not a short, simple process.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, explained and some things like Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and general law enforcement services the County cannot fund by assessment.
Commissioner Adkinson stated at the tail end of what Mr. Liesenfelt said, he said that the County cannot fund, some things are court defined as core services; if she heard him, he said once this is voted on, then they might stick it back in; and she asked if the Board voting for something it does not actually understand.
Mr. Liesenfelt responded the amendment is not comprehensive in the Bill that they passed; and if it passes, they are going to have to have an implementation session on how to implement it; this is him talking; and that is where the sausage is being made.
Chair Altman stated if the County cuts Parks and Recreation, the youth program, it will definitely have to spend more money on law enforcement jails.
Mr. Liesenfelt noted could be.
Attorney Richardson inquired if the Board would like to receive a brief update on the ruling in the case on the ballot language from today.
Chair Altman responded absolutely.
Mr. Liesenfelt expressed his thanks.
Chair Altman stated and then Mr. Liesenfelt can finish if there are any other questions.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she is sorry to interrupt Mr. Liesenfelt.
Chair Altman asked if Mr. Liesenfelt was finished, he can wait until . . .
Mr. Liesenfelt replied he can finish up afterwards.
Attorney Richardson commented as the Board knows as Mr. Liesenfelt sent out the notice earlier, Leon County Circuit Court Judge today declared the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3 to be clearly and conclusively defective; among the issues with the ballot title and summary was that the ballot title, the court found that it was more akin to a political slogan and that the Save Our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes was not fair and neutral, then invoking Save Our Homes borrowed the brand of the assessment cap that the Board is familiar with, and for other reasons that it was more political rhetoric and not neutral or not an explanation; also found the summary to be defective in its structure and language; the summary states that the amendment benefits Florida taxpayers by and then list a number of things; first and foremost was ensuring funding for core services; what the court found was that the amendment does not ensure funding for anything, including those core services that have been discussed, because by shrinking the local tax base it is likely to decrease the revenues available to local governments even to fund those core services; and that is the court’s analysis of the title and summary. He continued by saying it has been sent back to the Attorney General (AG) who has 10 days to rewrite the ballot title, and then there will be 10 days from that for anyone to mount a challenge; the State could also appeal from this ruling, so that is the current status; and all of that said, Amendment 3 will be on the ballot, it is just this particular title and summary that were at issue in the case.
Chair Altman mentioned he just received his sample ballot, and he asked how that will work with ballots about to be printed.
Attorney Richardson replied that is why . . .
Chair Altman interjected by saying Commissioner Feltner, who is in the middle of this, probably knows when all of the ballots are being printed.
Commissioner Feltner advised the ballots for the general is what is being talked about, and those will not be printed until after the primary; he thinks there is some period in time, maybe 10 days or something like that, to certify the election and all those things; and he does not think the design for the ballot even happens until the very beginning of September.
Chair Altman stated so it will be early September.
Commissioner Feltner pointed out because of Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA), so that is 45 days ahead of an election is when military ballots and overseas ballots have to go, so that have a small window there to certify the election results from the primary before they start printing ballots again; he reiterated definitely the early part of September; and obviously, Tim Bobanic, Supervisor of Elections, is not here so he does not want to answer on his behalf, but he thinks he has a good understanding on that.
Mr. Liesenfelt stated it is not on a slide, he just wants to conclude with a couple of points; if the voters approve this, they as staff, they have not sat down with the directors, but he could see on November 3rd if the voters approve it, after November 3rd, the County would be looking at some kind of targeted hiring freeze; it will still hire bus drivers and Road and Bridge operators, because those are needed to keep operating; staff would look at what needs to be done; and they could possibly place a hold on capital projects that have not started yet to see what the impact is and make sure the County can continue to fund them. He went on to say staff will be sitting down quickly to have a consultation with the Board on what to do; the interesting thing is, there will be a new Board; the last meeting, he believes, is this Board’s constituted is November 10th; the next Board gets sworn in November 17th, so it will probably be after Thanksgiving, but staff would be asking the Board to sit down; and he even wrote it this way, “Final Note, if Amendment 3 is passed, the impacts and reduction of services that the citizens will feel will happen before October 1st.” He noted good staff members will get laid off, they will leave before October; it is not an 11-month at that point; the Board will see the effects throughout 2027; and just to repeat, staff did write a six or seven-page report, which is attached to the Agenda Item for anyone to take a look at.
Chair Altman stated one of the questions he had and do not know if they got a clear answer on it or not, the Board talked about this; the County’s ad valorem bond issues, and he is sure throughout the State there have been quite a few bonds that have been issued; those bonds have been issued based on a homestead exemption at a certain amount, it goes to 250; and he asked what happens if the ability to pay those bonds is compromised because of a lower assessment, and if anyone knows.
Mr. Liesenfelt replied he is not the expert on that one; he would say bond obligations are a core service, but Chair Altman is right, the revenue could still be going down; at some point the County would have an effect on its ability to bond, its rates would go up; and he reiterated obviously, its rates will go up because the County has less guarantee to the bonds.
Chair Altman stated so the Legislature has an implementation session, so he guesses the answer they may give is the problems that are created that would go before the Legislature and they will . . .
Mr. Liesenfelt interjected by saying he hopes so.
Chair Altman noted hopefully be able to fix some of those.
Commissioner Feltner commented he thinks always the Board’s understanding when talking about the debt, the debt must be serviced, shall be serviced, so existing bonds have to be repaid; he thinks the question of rates and those sorts of things would be on any kind of future ability, because that certainly could be influenced by the County’s ability to service debt in the future; he reiterated whatever exists today that the County services will continue to be, right; and he does not think there is anything in there that says the County does not have debt obligation because of this and the referendum.
Mr. Liesenfelt mentioned and it is a core service; at least in paying off with ad valorem, General Fund ad valorem, the County’s debt service is $2.8 million a year, so it is not for the County, it is in decent shape; there are Utilities, Solid Waste, have some debt out there; but they are not general ad valorem funding.
Commissioner Adkinson state this original homestead thing was designed to keep people in their houses; looking at it, if the County has to bring in money other ways, then it is still going to come out of the pockets of the people who suddenly do not have this anymore; and she is just concern that it is not doing what they wanted it to do.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation to the County Manager for the update; he stated the County will just follow this as it moves on; he certainly agrees with the general intent; the State needs to fix some problems with the property tax issues; he asked if this is the solution; and he advised it could be problematic.

action_text: Rick Heffelfinger stated his concern with this one is that in the recent past, there was a water main break, he thinks, or some service that needed to be done; there was a boil water notice that went up north, and this project is up north; he understands the County is going to be shutting down a pretty major line to divert into the new line and isolate the old line, if he has that right; his concern is that there was a disconnect in communication with up north, from what he heard, that they were not notified, the water just went out, they did not know if they were going to have to boil water; and people are at work, the water is out, they do not know if when the water goes out that he or she does not have fire protection, as far as he knows. action_text:
Richard Heffelfinger stated this sounds like a public hearing to amend the Barefoot Bay Utility Services rates; there were some people here last month that he thinks were quite adamant that the Board needs to give them some relief; he does not know if this gives them 100 percent relief, but it is good news; it is going to reduce their rate back at least to last year, so he thinks that is good; there is a fiscal impact, it does not say there is; and when it rolls back to 2025, he guesses there was a study that was done that identified that phasing out of the Barefoot Bay was not going to cost that high of a rate, because all of those monies that were being collected, partially because of that rate, he thinks was to maintain that plant. He went on to say he hopes the Board just keeps it on its last legs until it phases out; it does not say how much revenue is being lost due to that rollback; again, that is probably an enterprise fun thing, and does he care; he does not know, it just seemed like a reducing rates and not showing how much rate loss there was; and he was just a little bit concerned about that.
Chair Altman stated why the Board does not do this, if Mr. Heffelfinger is finished, there are 11 cards on this Item, maybe have staff give a quick summary of it; maybe some of the questions could be answered; and a lot of people showed up from Barefoot Bay to be heard.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated he thinks there was a multi-year rate increase that everybody was squawking, he does not know what it rolled all that back; and he thinks that was almost complete or did complete last year.
Chair Altman stated to let the staff give a presentation.
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, explained at the last Board meeting, the Board approved for the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to be sunset, effective in January 2030; that is based on the last bond payment associated with Barefoot Bay being made in December 2029; and when staff does rate calculations, they are always looking at read calculations for the entity to be around for perpetuity.
Chair Altman asked if everybody can hear.
Mr. Fontanin asked if he should start over.
Chair Altman replied yes.
Mr. Fontanin reiterated the last Board meeting, the Board approved for the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District to be sunset in January 2030; the rationale of that is that the last bond payment associated with the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District occurs in December 2029; based on that Board action, staff looked at, along with the rate consultant, an analysis of looking at what the needed revenue would be in order to sustain itself until the 2030 sunset period; based on that, they did an analysis, they reviewed that the user rates could be rolled back to 2025, he believes that is a reduction of 4.8 percent; and they would flat line them there out. He noted in the Agenda Report, there are further redlines associated with it, so anytime a revision is made to a Resolution, it has to be shown through a red line process; when the rates were approved in 2022, the rates that are shown in redline, not only are they adjusted but basically they were shown to the 2025 rate, and the remaining rates they just made current from the 2022 to the 2026; in a nutshell, water and sewer user rates rolled back to 2025, at a 4.8 percent reduction; and they will be flat lined through 2030; come 2030, the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer accounts in the Water and Sewer District will get turned over to adopted to whatever the Countywide system is at that time.
Chair Altman advised this is not passing the rate, this is simply to advertise.
Mr. Fontanin stated that is correct, this is step one.
Commissioner Adkinson stated when she had people coming into her office saying the rates in Barefoot Bay are difficult; and she asked when the Board asked Mr. Fontanin to look at this, what did he anticipate the percentage rate increase being over the next three years prior to his relooking at it.
Mr. Fontanin responded by Board direction, staff used the Consumer Price Index (CPI) water and sewer maintenance index, so the last adjustment was 4.8 percent; and they look at it every November.
Commissioner Adkinson asked what they anticipated those increases to be.
Mr. Fontanin replied he would have to look at the number, but the way everything is going, he would anticipate another four or five percent increase.
Commissioner Adkinson inquired doing what the County is doing, if it is not only rolling it back, it is stopping those increases for the next three years.
Mr. Fontanin replied affirmatively; he stated if he is being asked him the way everything is going in the industry, the CPI is absolutely in a trajectory to keep going up; and Commissioner Adkinson is correct, they are kind of like flat lining it.
Dennis LaBelle commented he is here representing the unified group of Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer customers; they are here to address a clear legal contradiction in how Brevard County structures its water billing; it is specifically this Agenda Item; today the Board is voting on a proposal to decrease their water and sewer rates to the 2025 level, a 5.15 percent decrease; while any rate reduction is a step in the right direction, let them be clear that this tiny rollback is an inadequate Band-Aid that does nothing to alleviate the crushing weight of their bills; and it will not placate them. He pointed out for everyone who is watching, his bill is $110 for two people, and to compare that to his or her bills; between 2022 and 2026 Barefoot Bay Utility rates skyrocketed by a staggering 54 percent and rolling rates back by just one year leaves residents trapped under a compounding, massive financial penalty compared to the rest of Brevard County customers the County manages; a single-family residential home in Barefoot Bay is in an exact same consumer class as residential homes in Port St. John, Merritt Island, and Mims; and they flush the same water, require the same statutory environmental processing, and answer to the same Board of County Commissioners. He stated basically, a 54 percent increase rollback of 5.515 percent is not adequate; when they turned over the system, Barefoot Bay system, to the County, they were required to pay a fee; when new builders build these massive buildings; he asked if they are required to pay a fee to hook up; he stated it is just for my information; and he asked if he has to pay like $5 million to hook up to the system.
Chair Altman responded yes, there is an impact fee that new construction has to pay; and he asked staff to give a general idea of maybe where that is.
Mr. LaBelle asked if it is like $5 million or $10 million for $10,000 units.
Mr. Fontanin stated it is under a thousand dollars for water and sewer, and the exact amount he believes is about $700 or $800.
Mr. LaBelle asked if it was per toilet.
Mr. Fontanin replied per Equivalent Residential Connection (ERC), a single-family home equivalent.
Mr. LaBelle asked if for Barefoot Bay it would be $5,000.
Mr. Fontanin responded it is a calculation, so as he will see, they do the same calculation, so the Agenda Item will be later about the connection fees for Countywide; it starts off with a two-bedroom equivalent; and then staff uses the Administrative Code to do the calculation on anything that alters from that, whether it is higher or lower.
Chair Altman mentioned he appreciated Mr. LaBelle’s input; the Board is not voting on anything today other than advertising the ordinance, so it is not going to do any fees or increases; and this is only to have permission to advertise.
Denise Emmel stated she has a single-family home in Barefoot Bay, and her water bill is $94; she is the only one who lives there; she will not even power wash her house because of the water bill; despite the facts of their sameness, the County continues to carve Barefoot Bay Utilities customers out into an isolated billing island; even with this 5.15 percent decrease, their neighbors across the County will still pay a base sewer fee of $32.79, while they are charged a premium $54; and their consumption rate will remain highly inflated. She went on to say this is not a difference in usage, it is a geographical penalty; freezing or slightly rolling back these rates until 2029 does not solve the underlying injustice, only integrating them into the Countywide system sooner will truly help with their bills; all five of the Commissioners are equal in representing them and in being responsible for their water and wastewater; since buying their utility system 26 years ago, the customers have paid inflated rates; and she asked if 26 years long enough, must they wait another three and a half years to see real relief. She asked the Commission to stop delaying and integrate them into a single, equal County utility class immediately.
Karen Conrad remarked she would like to closely look at the administrative logic the County uses to justify the residents’ utility bills; Brevard County Utility Services is currently operating six wastewater treatment plants for five of those plants; the County operates a unified regional pricing structure; this means if a plant in Northern Brevard needs a multi-million dollar upgrade or a facility in the South Beaches faces high operational costs, these financial burdens are socialized across the entire County footprint; and the County does this because it recognizes that a unified utility network benefits the whole region’s health, ecology, and economy. She continued by saying when it comes to the sixth plant, their plant, Barefoot Bay, the logic just flips; suddenly, regional socialization stops and localized billing begins; and she asked why this principle of a shared infrastructure applies to only five plants, but ends at the borders of Barefoot Bay.
Chuck Barnett stated they have heard the response that the County’s hands are tied until existing utility bonds are paid off on December 31, 2029; respectfully, Commissioners, this is a bureaucratic excuse, not a legal barrier; bond obligations do not prevent the County from giving them operational equity today; it could vote to integrate Barefoot Bay into the Countywide system now by keeping the remaining bond payments as a transparent, temporary fix line item exclusively on Barefoot Bay’s bills until 2029; the existing debt will still be paid by the users of the system, and not one penny needs to be paid by other customers; and if current bond debt obligations does not prevent the County from blending rates from the rest of its system, it cannot be used as an excuse to isolate them. He noted the dual standard is administratively inconsistent; if this system is regional for five plants, it must be reasonable for all six; this is something the Board agreed to when it voted two weeks ago to integrate Barefoot Bay into the Countywide system; and it has no legal or logical basis to justify waiting until December 31, 2029.
Bonnie Carpenter commented she lived in the Pines for 23 years, now she lives in, and is a resident of, Barefoot Bay; she is here to challenge the accounting behind Barefoot Bay’s inflated utility rates; when a municipality isolates a single infrastructure asset for localized billing, the math almost always penalizes the captive ratepayer through the over allocation of the administrative overhead; they are paying a massive premium on their base facility charges; and she pays $110 a month, and she throws her dishwater out on her plants, so she does not get it. She mentioned they want to know exactly how much Central County overhead is being packed into that number; their billing is processed centrally by Brevard County Utility Services; their engineering is managed centrally; the executive legal teams and administrative staff are all located in Viera, funded by general utility revenues; and if they are paying higher rates to cover localized operational costs, but they are also being charged a percentage to support the County’s Central administrative apparatus, they are being double dipped.
Norman Perkins stated they are publicly requesting a transparent line item of the most recent cost service study; they want proof that revenues collected by Barefoot Bay are staying entirely within their plant ecosystem, and are not actively subsidizing central staff or capital improvements of the other five blended facilities; in addition, they are publicly requesting a transparent line item audit going back to their utility increases from 2013, Resolution No. 13-002, and a transparent line item audit of increases from 2022, Resolution No. 22-001; and they want proof that the revenue collected from Barefoot Bay customers has been used for, and accounted for, the items in areas that were stated in the Resolutions that they were used. He explained his water bill was $186 last month, and it is unfortunate that he cannot even drink the water; he has a whole house filter system, which many people in Barefoot Bay also cannot drink the water there; they either buy the water, use it like that, or they have to have some kind of a filtration system; and it is unfortunate that he pays $186 and cannot even drink the water.
Ray Delorme stated he wants to bring this back to the human costs of this rate structure; the vast majority of the customers that use Barefoot Bay water and sewer system live in two manufactured home communities; a majority of these residents are retirees, Veterans, and individuals living on fixed social security incomes; their public utility designs are supposed to act as a form of social insurance; and it is meant to protect vulnerable populations from being financially wiped out by localized geographic or infrastructure challenges. He continued by saying over the last few years, while general County utility rate increases were managed at single digit percentages; Barefoot Bay was hit with compounding double digit annual increases; for someone on fixed income at $54 base rate just for wastewater is not just a minor inconvenience, it cuts directly into money needed for groceries, health care, gas, and insurance; he showed the Board a copy of his utility bill as an example of the unfairness; he noted on June 10 to July 10, 2026, the total current charges for 2,800 gallons of usage is $132; with rollback to the 2025 rates, the cost of this bill would be $125; and if this home was on Merritt Island, or another Countywide system, the cost would be $77, big difference. He stated the increase to the other Countywide customers, if the County integrated Barefoot Bay into the Countywide system, now would be $2 a month, or even less if the Barefoot Bay customers continue paying off existing bond debt, as they have proposed; again, he has been there since 2019 when they first moved there, their bill was $46 minimum that they had to pay; his last bill was $143; he asked where does the County go from $46 to $143; and he stated maybe the Board to figure that out and correct that for them.
Terry Brewer commented he has been a Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District customer for over 12 years; they are a captive consumer class, they cannot choose another sewer provider, they cannot dig their own septic tanks, and they are entirely at the mercy of this Board; forcing a fixed income retirement community to bear 100 percent of its localized infrastructure burden for another three and one-half years, while younger, wealthier, more developing parts of the County enjoy socialized blended rates is funnily unfair, it is unjust; it is fundamentally unaffordable for many of the residents in this system, including mobile home communities of Barefoot Bay and Snug Harbor; and they have been paying a lot more than everyone else in the County. He went on to say since the first double digit increases of 2022; they are not asking for a refund; and they just want the County to stop fleecing them.
Sydne James mentioned to wrap up their group’s presentation today, they want to look forward to the solution; they acknowledge that the County Commission has previously discussed and voted to move forward to sunset the independent Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer District, and by advertising today to roll back rates a tiny bit and promise they will not increase from now until they are integrated into the Countywide system; this is not a gift, she read the audit, they were overpaying and the audit said that, so the County gets to not raise it anymore and roll it back; and they are still paying on everything they owe on. She reiterated it is not a gift to charge them more; in fact, legally the County is not supposed to charge more than is required; these are tiny concessions the County is offering, and they do not solve the problem of the unfair and unaffordable rates for Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer customers; let them address the claim that this transition cannot happen until December 31, 2029, because of outstanding bond debt; this is legally incorrect; Florida law allows this Board to dissolve the District immediately; the County Attorney can tell the Board as much; the bond holders only care that their debt service is secured by the utilities revenue; and the County does not need to wait three and one-half more years, it can dissolve the District now, absorb Barefoot Bay into the unified County network, and immediately lower their base sewer rate from $54.28 to the Countywide standard of $32.79, or less, depending on the tier of customers. She stated to honor the remaining bond obligations simply place, as previously stated, a transparent, temporary debt service surcharge as a separate line item exclusively on the Barefoot Bay customer bills; this allows them to pay off their outstanding bond debt without being forced to suffer under unaffordable fees for the next three and one-half years; she asked the Board not to let this transition drag out through years of artificial bureaucratic delay; she noted they have stated the legal inconsistency, the mathematical and unfairness, and the clear path to an immediate financial compromise; the Board has the ability to reconsider or repeal its vote from two weeks ago and update the timeline for integration of their utility system; and they ask for a concrete timeline and an expedited vote to finally bring regional utility equity to Barefoot Bay by the end of 2026.
John Requa provided the Board with a handout; he stated he agrees with his fellow residents, and it is nice to see them here; Barefoot Bay is a wonderful place to live, except for the water; that is why they are fighting so hard, they love it there; what he has provided the Board, he asked for this via email and he has come here he does not know how many times that Commissioner Adkinson had this done by the council for going over the prices, the cost, the debt, and everything, the Barefoot Bay Water and Sewer; he read it twice, and he understands a little; the Board will see some questions on its page, and they are for Mr. Fontanin, Commissioner Adkinson, and someone from the council that did this survey; and they are requesting that the Commission comes to Barefoot Bay, send appointment out with the Board of Trustees, it has been done before with a town hall meeting, and explain the audit as it is difficult to understand. He pointed out as an example, there will be questions that he has; he has more as he reads it; but one cannot get it will the three minutes of democracy that it has; he is confused about the cost of the bond when it started, how many bonds were involved, he heard there were at least two, he is confused about how much is collected; the highlighted stuff the Board sees on the pages are answers he received from the audit, he put that on there; he sees the total take in per year is $7,760,587; it is hard looking at that, and he wants to know where the money goes; he would still like to know what the estimated cost is for the consumer when the County goes on the new plan, it has to have an idea of what that is going to be; and there cannot be a forecast unless the County knows what it is going to charge. He mentioned he wants to make sure that none of their funds or what they are paying now are going towards that new facility, since they are going to be liberated and be a part of Brevard County, which they do not feel like they are right now; a separate district is what he keeps hearing; that is his request; he agrees with his fellow citizens; this is amazing, he used to come by himself a couple of years, and this is just heart lifting; he really would like the County to get in touch with the Trustees and set a meeting up; he is requesting that very strongly; there is nothing wrong with transparency, there is nothing wrong with answering questions; and they still disagree with the decision the County made, but it does not mean the questions cannot be answered.
Mr. Heffelfinger advised he would like to come back up because the Board cut him off.
Commissioner Adkinson advised he did not get cut off.
Mr. Heffelfinger asked if he did not get his three minutes, and he wants to play back the tape.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she will make sure the questions will get answered if they have not gotten answered.

action_text:
Brad Molander commented he is an Artificial Intelligence (AI) engineer during the day and he volunteers at Brevard Soccer Academy in the evenings; the reason why he is here tonight, he does not want to take up too much time, but with the property tax on the agenda for this fall and its potential ramifications to the County, he was curious on what modeling had been done for impacts to Parks and Recreation; he noticed the County had some numbers created, and he was wondering if staff has had a plan on the Parks and Recreation side on how that might impact the youth programs; as a reminder, he got into this by one day showing up at his daughter’s soccer practice, and they say, “Hey, we need a coach”, so one volunteers and does it; and he kind of got sucked into the whole thing because when he was little he was in youth soccer and it kind of gave him the opportunities that he has in his life. He went on to say one of the great things about Brevard Soccer Association (BSA) specifically, and other area clubs, is that they are a non-profit organization, so they are here exclusively for the community, to get kids off of iPads, get them outside; as of last spring, they have 1,600 kids in their program; one of the things they are looking at is how those services potentially could impact the club, the parks, but also the families; they have a lot of kids that they subsidize that cannot afford to play soccer; they get them in the club, put them on the field, get them shoes, and get them out there; it is a sight to see if any of the Commissioners are ever near Max Road in the evenings in the fall or spring semester, he or she will see a lot of kids out there having the time of their lives; and that is all due to the volunteers that do it. He expressed his appreciation for all that Parks and Recreation has done for the club up to this point, it has been wonderful; he noted it is a great partnership that they have; that is his root question, what modeling has been done, what impacts are there, and is Parks and Recreation open to talking with some of the area clubs so they could start making provisions to help understand what those impacts could be; their season runs starting right now and goes through right at the end of November; and in February, they fire up again. He expressed his appreciation to the Board for everything it does do in the day in and day out.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated he is looking at Ian Golden, Parks and Recreation Director, so he is going to catch Mr. Molander; he will highlight that $18 million number, that is $11 million of General Fund that would not be eligible because it is not a core service, and that $7 million number is the reduction due to less taxable values in the Multiple Services Taxing Units (MSTUs); there are three or four, he forgets the exact number, of park MSTUs; and each part of the County is a little bit different.
Mr. Golden explained the quick answer is if someone requests information, some factual information about what the potential impacts are, they can have a conversation; there is that State law that restricts County employees while they are on the clock from starting conversations; he will not take a position one way or the other, but he will be happy to have a conversation with him; and he was going to catch him on the way out and basically tell him the same thing.
Mr. Molander stated again, it is just a reminder, he guesses it will be helpful; there are a lot of area clubs like theirs, they are not even the largest one, 1,600 kids is a lot of kids; and he thinks it would be helpful to open those lines of communication so they can help work with the parents, because they are getting questions as well.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she feels his pain, and she has a lot of concern, too; and she asked if the Board is allowed to, if this gets implemented next year, to have new voter-approved referendums just for Parks.
Mr. Liesenfelt responded the short answer is any new referendum would have to be at a general election, so that would push it to 2028; and it would not be able to help the first year of reduction.
Commissioner Pritchett explained she does agree with Chair Altman on this, they are taking a lot of this out on the kids, and she has great concern for that herself.
Chair Altman commented those are very good questions, and as County goes through this, hopefully it will have more answers; the problem staff has is they are under the gun; if they try to answer a question, then they are going to be accused of advocating for or against the referendum, so they have to be careful; he really appreciates his question, because if the public is asking for a question, the Board is not preempting he or she prior to having a question; it should have the ability to answer objective questions, how much money, how much is lost, and how does the County replace that; those questions are really good; and he asked the public to please keep them coming.
Sandra Sullivan mentioned she runs a group called Waves Action, and the focus is on accountability and transparency; she has a couple of comments on Amendment 3 on this referendum; coming into this budget time, she and others ask that the Board does some cutting costs of wasteful spending; the sentiment that she has seen on Waves Action are people are pissed off that the spending keeps going up without restraint; the County has the highest assessments, the highest growth, and it has a lot of growth revenue coming in; and the budget went from $1.83 million in 2022 to $2.83 million in 2025, a pretty substantial increase. She stated she is going to just say her disappointment in the last meeting with Commissioner Pritchett coming on this Board; the motion that was taken on the budget to bust the cap, with Commissioner Feltner voting for that, the only no vote was former Commissioner Delaney, to direct staff, and Commissioner Feltner asked staff to clarify if they were preparing two budgets; one to put up there that was not busting the cap, and one not to bust the cap; no, it was clarified they were only preparing a budget to bust the cap; in the last meeting a budget was put up that did not bust the cap, and then at the last minute Chair Altman takes a vote on a different budget with no accountability and transparency, no documents online, and the vote was taken to bust the cap; and she reiterated she is not too happy about that. She pointed out that in coming here for many years there has been the request to cut the Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRAs) that had no debt; no, the County gave $12.1 million to a friend who wants to build through a CRA to build a hotel parking lot, parking building; it did not take action on impact fees; it kicked the can down the road on that; it did not cut waste; she advised the Board do not vote to put Save Our Indian River Lagoon (SOIRL) on because it may need this if this Amendment 3 passes for infrastructure needs; no, the Board went ahead and put that on there; she hopes people vote no; she asked the Board at this time to go and look at that budget, cut waste, cut costs, and cut where it needs to; Commissioner Atkinson did a very good list of things that could be cut; there is a lot of wasteful spending; and it is time to take action on that now before this budget goes through or the County is just digging itself deeper.
