title: PUBLIC HEARINGS

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing to consider a resolution adjusting connection fees for South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area.
Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, stated Item H.1. is to amend the Utility Services Rate Resolution adjusting connection fees for South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area; as the Board can see in the Agenda Item a clean version and a red line version; to just go over the redline version, the core of it is that staff made the adjustments to the connection fee to get current from the 1993 to current; in addition, they also took the liberty of doing some definition revisions; some of the small service fees like towing service; they made some minor adjustments from like $50 to $75, and of that magnitude; but the big component with regard to this is the water sewer connection fee and seeking approval.
Richard Heffelfinger commented the County did a big blow up on 7-7-26; he was really pissed off on 7-7-26, because this was extremely confusing; he will give Mr. Fontanin and his gang credit, the attachments were cleaned up quite nicely; there are no more dock files, no more confusion that this was only connection fees; what he would have loved to have had the first time was this, this study right here would have caused that confusion to go away; he asked why it is left only at the public hearing, because the public cannot study it, he does not know; and if he was a conspiracy theorist, he would say the County held out until the end. He went on to say this study was conducted on October 22, 2025, and it should have been attached at the time that conversation was had; the County wasted a lot of his time and its own he thinks; he thinks it was not a clean . . . and he is glad to see it cleaned up, and he will give Mr. Fontanin credit for that; he would hope his complaining would have had something to do with that, maybe, maybe not, but he will take that; and this is connection fees and to jam it to them, he is 100 percent in favor.
Commissioner Pritchett advised she did not get the privilege of working through this with the rest of the Commission, so she is not going to vote to support this; she would have supported spreading it out over a five-year period of time to just check and see how much it might have maybe knocked the County out of the market of new housing; and she is just letting the Board know this, that is going to be her vote.
Chair Altman asked if there is a motion.
Commissioner Feltner stated he is waiting to see what the Commission is going to do here; and maybe there is more discussion needed.
Commissioner Adkinson noted as Mr. Heffelfinger said, staff cleaned it up; a lot of work was done on it, staff took a lot of time; she is ready to support this thing because of the work that they have done; and she supports connection fees on new builds.
There being no further comments or objections, the Board adopted Resolution No. 26-063, amending the Utility Services Rate Resolution encompassing South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area, adjusting the fees once from the current fees to the full amount of the recommended connection fees, to be implemented on October 1, 2026.
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Amend the Utility Services Rate Resolution adjusting connection fees for South Beaches, Merritt Island, North Brevard, Port St. John, and the South Central Mainland Service Area.

action_text:
Chair Altman called for a public hearing to consider an ordinance amending Chapter 102, Article IV, Division 3 of the Brevard County Code to make data centers ineligible for Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemptions.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, explained Item H.2. is an ordinance amending Chapter 102, Article IV, Division 3 of the Brevard County Code to make data centers ineligible for economic development ad valorem tax exemptions; at the April 7, 2026, regular meeting, the Board approved legislative intent and permission to advertise an ordinance to make data centers ineligible for those tax exemptions; that was approved at the time; it took a while because of a previous amendment to the Code that had not been incorporated by Municode into the County’s codified ordinances, so had to take some measures to make sure that this is codified correctly if the Board enacts it, but it is before the Board tonight; and the proposed ordinance provides a definition for the term data center, which is drawn from Federal and State law, further provides the data centers are ineligible for the economic development ad valorem tax exemption program.
Richard Heffelfinger remarked this has been hanging out since April, so he is glad to finally see it show up; the fiscal impact is an interesting statement, because it says the correlation is that the lack of incentive may cause the developer to locate to another Florida county or state; Brevard County will receive no new ad valorem and tangible personal property tax revenues from this project; that was exactly the objective of doing this was to give them no reason to want to come here; people have heard all of the news, it is a hot topic, it is a hot thing for everybody; and there may be a big boom at the construction phase, but then the County would eat it on the water, the electricity usage, and the public’s going to bear a large part of that. He mentioned he does not think that is disputed, he thinks that is fact now; the Chinese is going to beat the US at Artificial Intelligence (AI), he doubts it; that is just not something that he thinks as a taxpayer and as a resident here that he does not want to bear that cost, and he does not think anybody does; they can be stuck out in the middle of nowhere where there is plenty of water; the County does not have plenty of water; people know that, they have been telling that for years, and yet, the County is still building like crazy, but that is a different topic; he asked if Brevard has one nuclear power plant; and it should get some more if it wants to play with data centers, so he thinks the intent here was good, but the intent is not complete. He noted the Board is going to hear some requests for a motion to ask for a moratorium, they have more time to look at it, because he does want to . . . they say that these things are fact; he asked are they truly facts; what is the water; he stated the Board should hear some people say, no, man, they fill up the chillers and they reuse the water, so they are not really a big water drain; but that is not . . . he heard that one place, he does not know if it is true or not; time to think about it would be good time to spend; since they are probably not going to want to come here; and to say the County is going to write them off completely, that is not fair either, but he does not want to incentivize them. He pointed out a moratorium would allow this issue to be settled and studied better to decide exactly what the impacts are; that is a good way to put that on hold and have more data come together, because a lot of people are digging it and there are going to be technology changes; maybe some of this heat factor, electronics incredible jumps and bounds; the County is doing now what it could not, unthinkable 10 years ago; maybe that data center problem goes away, and maybe Brevard could have data centers; until that happens, sometime needs to be spent to think about it; and he would like to see a move for a motion to have a moratorium, bring back an ordinance language for that, so more time can be spent on this before somebody drops a big problem in the County’s lap.
Chair Altman asked before Mr. Heffelfinger leaves, if under Senate Bill 180 is the County allowed to pass a moratorium; he was under the impression that . . .
Attorney Richardson advised it could be problematic with regard to Senate Bill 180.
Chair Altman stated the Board can get an opinion for that later, but it is one of the . . .
Mr. Heffelfinger interrupted by saying no a motion, take a motion to look at it would be a good start.
Sandra Sullivan expressed her appreciation to the Board for putting this on the Agenda to remove the data center tax exemption for the Economic Development Commission (EDC) tax abatement; the citizens are also asking for a two-year moratorium on hyperscale data centers; yesterday, Flagler County and Lakeland passed moratoriums on data centers, while Edgewater passed a permanent ban; Ormond Beach votes tonight, and Palm Beach and Dixie County meeting on August 6th; there are about 20 counties and cities Florida wide; in advance of that, she spoke at the last meeting, that have a moratorium; as the Board knows, the Governor race has really heated up over this issue; and she wants to just go over a little bit about the past performance on this particular issue. She went on to say Brevard County voted to approve the legislative intent on April 7th; Brevard did not go to legislative intent before the vote on December 17th, which gave the data centers 20-year tax exemption under Florida Statute 196.1995; Brevard County voters passed the referendum on November 5, 2024; they voted for specific, strictly bound constitutional authority; the Statute dictates any ad valorem tax exemption granted by the County Board under this program cannot exceed 10 years; and it should not have been approved in the first place. She stated on November 5, 2024, when voters approved the tax exemption abatement, voters would probably not have voted for it if the Board had put in a 20-year tax exemption on data centers; right after on December 17, 2024, right before Christmas when everybody is busy, when former Commissioner Feltner was on the EDC board and Chair of this Commission; the Ordinance was changed for a 20-year tax exemption; as established by Florida Statute 125.66, an ordinance cannot be changed without going out for legislative intent, as the Board did for this Item, for voter-referendum; she came here and spoke about this; and she is grateful that the Board has taken action on this. She stated data centers concern the public very much, the hyperscale; she hopes the Board will consider also doing a moratorium; two years, not a long time, but enough time to evaluate; her understanding is the EDC has some proposals in front of them; as the Board knows, the EDC gets a 12-month exemption on public records by the law that the State has done; they do not even get to find out what is really going on, but they know what is going on because she has done enough records requests to see that the EDC is already working on this issue; and she hopes the Board will approve this Item today and correct that record.
Steve Burdett stated in his retirement, he has kind of had a lot of time to see what is going on with these data centers throughout the country, and he knows a lot of people have had concerns over basically what happens to the water availability, what happens with their utility bills, and the same with electricity; he is especially concerned about the noise, especially for those who have to live by these things; and he knows from his experience, he believes the County has a Noise Ordinance, but he is not sure how it applies to a business of this nature. He continued by saying the other concern he expressed, and this was even before a lot of these data centers were built, was, and this was more at the national level, not necessarily the Board, but what happens to these data centers, the County has these redevelopment areas that were supposed to be used to take care of blight; he asked if these data centers ends up becoming outdated, who is going to take them down, who is going to get rid of them, and are they going to be an eyesore; is that part of these people have to do when they decide to build these data centers; and he reiterated he just wanted to express his concerns. He mentioned he knows a lot of people throughout the country have had concerns about it, and he would just assume they do not start here, or if they do that the County makes sure that they are governed properly.
Commissioner Pritchett stated she wanted to make a motion to approve; and Commissioner Feltner seconded the motion.
Attorney Richardson stated the Agenda is phrased as ‘consider adopting’, and he asked if the Board would mind phrasing that in just a, adopt the proposed ordinance, is that the motion.
Commissioner Pritchett responded affirmatively.
There being no further comments or objections, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 26-11, pertaining to the Brevard County Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption Program; amending Chapter 102 – Taxation, Article IV – Ad Valorem Property Taxation, Division 3; Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption Ordinance, Brevard County Code of Ordinances; amending Section 102-184 – Definition of Terms; amending Section 102-185 – Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption Established; providing for resolution of conflicting provisions; providing for severability; providing for an area encompassed; providing for an effective date; and providing for inclusion in the Code of Ordinances.

action_text:
Kathy Wall, Central Services Director, tonight the Board is here to discuss State Lobbying Services, and Steve Crisafulli is here to discuss his annual report.
Steve Crisafulli, representing SBM Partners, stated as the Agenda says, it is about the State lobbying contract, but it was never discussed regarding the legislative session; they discussed potentially doing that in July; and he expressed his appreciation to the Board for its grace in allowing them to do it at this meeting. He went on to say in a nutshell, he sent each of the Commissioners a breakdown of the legislative session; if he or she did not get it from him, maybe Ms. Wall or the County Manager sent that to the Commissioners; this year was the early session year where session starts in January, finishes in March, and yet again, this year they finished the session without a budget; the Governor called the Legislature back in session in the middle of May to work on a budget; at that time, after a little over two weeks, they were able to pass $117.5 billion budget, which is one-half of a billion dollars less than what it was two years ago, so they did pull down; and with that, they put $18 million into rainy day fund, so the Legislature is tightening its belt in these tougher economic times. He noted out of that, this session, they went in as a County with 12 appropriations requests across a range of spectrum of transportation issues, water issues, and they were able to get six of those funded; two of those did end up getting vetoed in the end; all in all, the County ended up with $6.87 million that was funded from the Legislature; $500,000 of that was vetoed; the two items that were vetoed were the multi-basin study at Miramar Road, Martin Road, and Fisk Boulevard, and then the signal at Caddington Drive and Stadium, which all are very aware of; along with the County’s request, the Sheriff did put a request in this year for $5 million for his Animal Care Center, which they were able to get the full appropriation on that, as some of the Commissioners were at the groundbreaking, he believes it was last week; and then, beyond that, the County, through the transportation work program and the different grants that brought in $281.5 million to the County to fulfill those needs. He pointed out besides that, it was a very slow year with regard to legislation; this year there was 1,896 measures that were filed and only 237 that were passed; 192 of those were general bills, so for those that have been familiar with that process, that is a very slow year; that is a lot of battling back and forth between the House and Senate on coming to terms on agreeing on the different issues; and he thinks the greatest victory of all that the County had is being able to secure the funding that they did based on a budget that is smaller than it was two years ago, and knowing that there are less resources in the different buckets that they create, that can go out to the counties. He mentioned the Governor did end up vetoing just under a billion dollars; of that, as he told the Board, $500,000 of it were issues that the County asked for funding on, and then Commissioner Adkinson has an issue near and dear to her, the Senate Bill (SB) 180 glitch Bill that the Senate passed unanimously, but the House did not take it up; everybody wonders why; there is a lot of internal politics on that; he does know, in speaking with the Senate sponsor, that he is intending to bring that back again next year; and under new leadership, the Board may see a House that is more interested in that issue this time around. He stated with that, again, he would send the Board the information on some of the different bills that may impact the County with regard to growth management, water resources, transportation, and those types of things; and he would be happy to answer any questions.
Chair Altman expressed his appreciation to Mr. Crisafulli for presenting to the Board, and for the hard work he puts in during the legislative session.
Mr. Crisafulli expressed his appreciation to the Board for all of its communication throughout session; he or she is always there to answer a call; he knows several of the Commissioners, which he has talked to several times during session when there questions, especially with the property tax issue on the ballot; he knows Attorney Richardson may have mentioned this, but the Attorney General does have 10 days to either appeal or change that language; they will know in very short order what that is going to look like, and if there is an appeal that does take place and how it is accepted versus the language change; and that is in short order for sure.
Chair Altman asked what happens if they do not agree, if the court rules again that it is improper.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, replied they start to run out of time to get language through that is approved, but Amendment 3 will be one there; he is sure they will get to a place where it is . . .
Chair Altman interjected by saying will the court write the language.
Attorney Richardson responded he does not believe so.
Sandra Sullivan stated she appreciates Mr. Crisafulli is former House Speaker, has a great deal of knowledge up in Tallahassee and brings a lot of expertise; however, on the Agenda there is an option to go out to Request for Proposals (RFP); she does think that is the appropriate thing to do; she is going to say there are a few conflicts on that recent 222-unit development, he was the lobbyist, she understands, from online for that particular project and also with Health First; it does present a few potentially conflicts of interest; and she also has a bit of heartburn with, what was it, $35,000, she does not know as it has been a while. She went on to say that went to the Political Action Committee (PAC) when Commissioner Feltner was running . . . thanks to Commissioner Feltner for fighting for the Lagoon, stuff; the County tried three times to get him as the County Lobbyist from Ron Book; she just feels that the fair and equitable thing is to go out for RFP, see what comes in, and make an informed decision with everything at hand; he is not negating his abilities, but she would just like to say one thing she came up here and asked about; there are $130 to $197 million costs that the County is looking at putting on ‘we the people’ for the connection by Space Florida; she thinks the Feds and the State need to pay for that; that is a significant amount of money that a promise was made here that that burden would not be put on the ratepayers; yet, the budget indicates it is going to be put on the ratepayers probably after the election; she asked if that is right; and she noted it is not so good optics that really needs to be prioritized for funding so not to put that on them.
Commissioner Pritchett expressed her appreciation to Mr. Crisafulli for all of the work he has done; she stated as far as a lobbyist, she thinks he is hitting it out of the park; she appreciates him having so many connections in the State of Florida; he is nice, so they listen to him, and that is an extra bonus; she expressed her appreciation for Mr. Crisafulli not raising his rates; and she noted there are a lot of pluses to that. She advised she has a quick question; she is sure this is not an issue because she asked the County Attorney about this; there is not a conflict on the things that he is doing other work on as far as the job the County has Mr. Crisafulli doing; and she asked if that is correct, although those guidelines are pretty . . .
Attorney Richardson explained there are two prohibitions in the current Contract; one prohibits SBM from lobbying where the Board of County Commissioners, where there is a conflict of interest; there is another that is just a blanket prohibition against SBM lobbying on behalf of private entities before the Board, regardless of whether there is an actual conflict of interest; that is more of a optics provision than an ethics provision; and if that remains within the Contract, then in his opinion, Mr. Crisafulli, in his capacity as a partner at SBM would not, consistent with the Contract, be able to lobby on behalf of private entities before the Board, so the Board may wish to consider whether to keep that prohibition in or to eliminate it and leave only the prohibition of lobbying when there is an actual conflict of interest.
Commissioner Pritchett asked how long Mr. Crisafulli has lived in Brevard County.
Mr. Crisafulli replied 55 years.
Commissioner Pritchett pointed out he is fighting for his home.
Commissioner Feltner expressed his appreciation to Mr. Crisafulli for all he has done for the County; he stated he thought Mr. Crisafulli would take this moment to tell the Board about what it should anticipate with the implementing language; the referendum was talked about tonight a little bit; maybe while the Commissioners are all here together, he can tell he or she that is going to happen in December; that is going to be during the organizational session; it will be a special session; and he asked what might be anticipated, that process, looking like.
Mr. Crisafulli stated Attorney Richardson actually touched on it; the reality is there is a session of implementation when the language is being put together; they have done this many a time on Statewide initiatives that the Legislature has to come back and work on; the nuance to this one is the State is going to have a new Governor that will have been elected in November, and there is an organizational session that starts November 18th; the likelihood of a special session for implementation, should it pass, would take place likely at that point in time, or during the first committee week that they have now set in the first week of December; the question is does the current governor want the ability to set the standard on what this initiative is going to be while working with the Legislature, because it is important to recognize the Governor does not pass legislation, he just approves it or denies it; and in this case, it is an implementation of a Statewide amendment. He pointed out he does not know the answer to whether or not the Governor gets a final say-so on what the initiative is; he is certainly going to have a foot in the ring when it comes to having this discussion, because this was his initiative to begin with; having said that, the State has two new legislative leaders, Senator Boyd and Speaker Garrison that will be coming in, and they have their own ideas as well; he is certain as they start polling this over the next couple of months, especially with the change in language, that will certainly change the dynamics around the ability for this to pass on the ballot; but as they start polling it, if they start seeing the likelihood that it is going to hit the threshold of 60 percent plus one, they will start formulating their ideas on how they are going to move forward. He commented right now, it is anybody’s guess; he can say this, the Board cannot, but polling always starts higher and finishes lower just because people become more educated, they understand, they hear the impacts it is going to have in their backyard; certainly, there is a conversation to be had on that around the State over the next couple of months; he would be remiss if he did not mention Leader Sirois and Senator Mayfield, in their help this year, helped sponsor each and every one of these budget initiatives and work diligently to get those passed; and he wants to make sure he gives them the proper credit, as well as incoming Senator Boyd who sponsored one of the dredging projects for them just because he likes Brevard County and wanted to see it have some success on that front, so he wanted to make sure he gives a little love to these folks. He reiterated there will be a session, it will be that all will be intimately involved in if in fact there is a conversation that has to take place if a ballot initiative passes.
Commissioner Feltner stated one-quarter of the Legislature changes every other year.
Mr. Crisafulli stated yes, that is correct, there are several people who will not be in that chamber that voted on this; admittedly, a lot of representatives voted on this to give the people a voice, they did not vote on it because they favored or disfavored it, they voted on it to give people a voice on it because it has to go in the Constitution due to the way it is drafted; probably some of them are glad they are not going to be there to implement to be honest; but the truth is, and Commissioner Feltner is right, one-third of that Legislature that put it in place will be there to implement it should they have that opportunity to do so.
Commissioner Feltner mentioned he thinks it is shocking to think one is sworn in, and within a couple of weeks of that, he or she is there for a special session to implement language that could be perhaps the most significant referendum that goes before the voters in quite a long time, so certainly challenges ahead of the Board; for all of those reasons, and for the good work that Mr. Crisafulli has done for the County, he would like to renew the Contract; and that would be his motion today.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she would second the motion.
Attorney Richardson asked if the Board would either address the issue of the prohibition on lobbying activities on behalf of private clients, or perhaps hear from Mr. Crisafulli on that issue.
Mr. Crisafulli stated there is a nuance to it as well; he does not represent SBM Partners when he represents the local clients that he does, he represents them through Crisafulli Consulting; he reiterated that is a nuance, Attorney Richardson is the legal mind, and he does not know how that interacts; he does not represent anyone before the County through SBM Partners; he only represents folks through his Crisafulli Consulting Company; and never in a way that is contrary to the stance that the County has on something, especially on a State issue as it is just not the way to do business. He went on to say he wants to be clear on that nuance, because he does have all of those folks contracted under Crisafulli Consulting.
Attorney Richardson commented he is just looking for the Board’s understanding of that provision and what the Board’s pleasure is with regard to that contractual issue, whether or not the Board is okay with Mr. Crisafulli doing that kind of representation; again, it is not an ethical conflict; that is already addressed by a separate prohibition; it is just a blanket ban on all lobbying on private activities in the Contract; and staff can clarify that, depending on the Board’s direction.
Commissioner Feltner stated he thinks Attorney Richardson said there was a clear conflict earlier, when a clear conflict presents itself.
Attorney Richardson advised just when there is a conflict that prohibition is in there, but that is not going to change; there is a secondary clause that no lobbying whatsoever, conflict or not, on behalf of a private client exists in the current SBM Contract; there are nuances to whether or not that applies to Mr. Crisafulli’s activities; but for staff’s direction moving forward, is the Board’s intention that the consultant and Mr. Crisafulli cannot lobby on behalf of those private interests even when there is no conflict, or would the Board be amenable to modifying the language.
Chair Altman stated it sounds like the Board needs to fix that to disallow lobbying if there is a direct conflict.
Commissioner Adkinson noted yes, she would agree with that.
Attorney Richardson stated staff can make that revision.
Commissioner Adkinson asked if there is a way the Board to structure the motion so it can make that clear.
Attorney Richardson responded if the motion incorporates that, just strike the blanket prohibition on lobbying activities and retain the prohibition on lobbying when there is a conflict of interest; and that will be enough direction.
The Board granted renewal of the Contract with SBM Partners; directed staff to strike the blanket prohibition on lobbying activities and retain the prohibition on lobbying when there is a direct conflict of interest; and authorized the Chair to execute the Contract.

action_text:
Juanita Jackson, Housing and Human Services Director, explained Item J.2. is a request for a letter of support for the Housing Authority of Brevard County for disposition of Lake View Pointe to Space Coast Community Development Corporation, a Housing Authority’s nonprofit affiliate; Lake View Pointe was constructed in 1964 and consists of 56 public housing units servicing low-income households; the property’s age, deteriorating infrastructure, and functional limitation is affecting the Housing Authority’s ability to provide quality housing efficiently; the Housing Authority development strategy is to transfer ownership of Lake View Pointe to Space Coast Community Development Corporation, request tenant protection vouchers and permission demo from Housing and Urban Development (HUD); once all tenants have been relocated, then demolish Lake View Pointe; Lake View Pointe redevelopment construction would be in late 2029 to mid-2030; future redevelopment will include no fewer than 56 affordable units; and subject to HUD’s approval and final relocation plan, the Housing Authority will provide affected residents with all notices, advisory services, relocation assistance, and moving assistance, and comparable housing opportunities required by HUD.
Richard Heffelfinger commented he does not usually get involved with public housing or any of that stuff, because . . . he will not get into any of that stuff to go into why he does not; this is confusing because he does not understand, it looks like the County is taking something that is funded by Brevard County through housing development dollars that are given, he guesses primarily by the State, and it is running this development, or it owns it; he asked if the County owns it; he noted so, the County owns it, maintains it as low . . . okay, the County does not own it, it manages it; no, it does not manage it; and he asked the County Attorney to keep going as he is learning more as he shakes his head. He stated he really appreciates trying to figure out what is going on because it looks like the housing wants to punt, and they want to punt to a private entity because there is some advantage punting to a private entity; as far as he knows, housing it is a nonprofit when it is kind of public housing; he asked if the County is punting; is it going to get some profit; is the County going to get some profit advantage by knocking it down, building it up; are the same number of units going to be replaced for low-income housing; are the costs going to be higher; and he stated it is going to be better, grant it.
Chair Altman stated to let the Board hear all of the cards, and staff will answer his questions and just who owns who.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated supposedly this outfit, Space Coast Community Development Corporation, is actually part of Housing Authority of Brevard County (HABC) now, yet it is still confusing; it sounds like who owns it now like talking about the water plant; he asked if the special district owns it or . . . so he is wary of that kind of shenanigans like what could possibly be the advantage; he advised somebody is going to get an advantage; and that are his questions.
Sandra Sullivan remarked in 1950 the County formed this entity of HABC; the Housing Authority of Brevard County as a quasi-governmental thing; when one looks up on Sunbiz, there is no such entity; by looking at who is, and she sent an email earlier, when going to Sunbiz, there are all of these businesses here at 1401 Guava Avenue in Melbourne, the location, which are these two of the entity of who the County wants to convey this property to that it says is a wholly-owned nonprofit affiliate, but then when looking up who this guy is, he is associated with a lot of developments, not just in Florida, but outside of Florida; and she is just going to say, this looks stinky. She pointed out it is like HABC does not exist, according to Sunbiz, and yet there are 374 properties that are all in the Housing Authority of Brevard County in the Property Appraisers, and then now the County is going to do something unprecedented; those are going to be put into another entity, but there is nothing to support that it is wholly-owned nonprofit affiliate; she asked the Board to defer this for today until there are additional documents put up; but she will just say, coming to these meetings for eight years, and the stink, she is just not happy with Commissioner Pritchett being back on the Board appointed, given some of the stinky stuff that has gone on that in having to come to these meetings and disclose that; $30 million to Driftwood, and she could make a long list of oh, no, she is looking at the Agenda again and rolling her eyes like not again; and the next four months are going to be hell she thinks, District 1.
Chair Altman advised he is actually looking forward to them.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, stated all staff is asking for, as the subject says on the Agenda, is a letter of support for the Housing Authority of Brevard County; they are not part of the County, they have the name Brevard County, they are not Brevard County; they are the Housing Authority one finds pretty much everywhere across the country; they have their own nonprofit to work on the development; and all they are doing is look for a letter of support from the County.
The Board authorized the Chair to execute a Letter of Support approving HABC’s proposed disposition of Lake View Pointe and transfer ownership to Space Coast Community Development Corporation.

Morris Richardson, County Attorney, stated that the August orientation for Value Adjustment Board (VAB) is part of the cycle each tax year; he just needs to the Board to elect two of its members to serve on that Board and who want to serve as Chair; currently, Commissioners Adkinson and Altman serve on the VAB, with Chair Altman serving as the Chair of the VAB.
Commissioner Adkinson asked if this is for the next . . .
Attorney Richardson interjected by saying this is for the next cycle that begins this month.
Chair Altman mentioned he is willing to continue, it is up to the rest of the Board.
Commissioner Adkinson stated she is willing to continue, but would really like Chair Altman to stay as Chair, only because he grabbed hold of the thing and nobody seemed to know what he or she was doing until he started asking questions.
Chair Altman noted he appreciated that and her willingness.
Commissioner Adkinson asked if Chair Altman would consider staying as VAB chair.
Chair Altman stated he will be willing to do that.
The Board reaffirmed Commissioners Altman and Adkinson as the liaison appointments for the 2026 VAB; and appointed Commissioner Altman as the Chair and Commissioner Adkinson as the Vice Chair of the VAB.

action_text:
Chair Altman stated the Board could maybe hear the applicants first; and he would love for them to maybe give a quick, simple summary of the promise this new technology may have in terms of environmental benefits, as well as giving land owners a choice, and maybe some of the new technology that he is excited about that is being brought to wastewater treatment.
Herschel Vinyard stated he and his colleague, Jeff Littlejohn, are here on the distributed wastewater issue; historically, the Board had three choices on how to get rid of domestic wastewater; there is septic, recognized it in Statute; in fact, adopted an expedited permitting process for distributing wastewater because they want to put this out in the field as fast as they can because the technology works; they want to get this permitted in lieu of septic tanks; and he continued by saying rather than sending all of the wastewater back to a central location, the wastewater is treated in a system and it is disbursed in one’s yard.
Chair Altman commented one of the things that truly excites him about this technology is that it is a fourth alternative that the County does not have; one of the things the County has is an on-site sewage treatment, septic tanks, they are put in, and then they just are in never-never land; one does not really know if they are working, or when they are failing; he remembers when he was in the Florida Senate when they passed the legislation really trying to grab a hold of the septic tank problem; it required annual inspections with a lot of fees; and it was a solution but not a solution like this. He mentioned it was very controversial because of the expense to the consumer because of the cost of having the impact of the cost of overseeing, regulating them, reviewing them, making sure they are working; the County is taking advantage of internet technology, digital technology, and maybe eventually Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology to have these septic facilities or the on-site wastewater treatment facilities that are continually monitored as they would in a public sewer treatment plant at very little cost; he thinks this is just the beginning of a new wave of how the County addresses its stormwater, septic impact problems, as well as there are some ways that this is even superior to sanitary sewer system; so often what happens in the times of hurricanes, storm surge, flooding where pump stations get overwhelmed, they back up which has happened numerous times; this could prevent that from happening because in the times of storms, most of that wastewater is confined into the tanks; and he reiterated, he is excited about it. He noted by looking at the Agenda Package, one can see that large portions of Brevard County is now under a moratorium due to a Federal judge where landowners have no option deprivation of their own personal private property rights; even very large sites are limited from use; this gives consumers an alternative; thirdly, he thinks ultimately, if the County does not fix this problem, there is going to be some significant impacts to its revenue stream; if at some point one cannot use his or her property, their three-acre site for anything, there will be some significant reductions in the County’s assessed valuation; he is excited about the future; and he thinks a County like Brevard, which is so state-of-the-art with space age technology, it is appropriate that Brevard becomes one of the leaders. He advised Mr. Vinyard did mention that there are other counties already embarking upon this and doing this technology.
Mr. Vinyard stated yes, sir, Lake County, which does not have a utility at all, has essentially banned septic tanks in most circumstances in their county; they are directing . . . say a new development comes along, like he said, they do not have a wastewater utility, and they direct it be distributed wastewater treatment as the solution; today, Santa Rosa County just signed on for this technology; they also do not have a wastewater utility, so they are excited about the technology; and there is an industrial computer that runs it. He went on to say the Chair Altman mentioned it is monitored 24/7 and controlled; and offsite a licensed wastewater treatment utility operator if they see that there is a problem with the system in one’s yard, he or she can actually override what goes on with the system and make sure the water is treated properly.
Chair Altman advised even if one has a leaky faucet or a toilet is running, the bells and whistles can go off, and that homeowner can be notified, it is really exciting.
Commissioner Pritchett asked what would be the difference between this and an advanced sewer system; she stated she is guessing it is a compact system, so she thinks this would be a good thing for the Board to understand; and she asked what the similarities, what the difference is, and which one does a better job.
Mr. Vinyard replied the biggest issue is the ability to monitor and control the system offsite where an advanced treatment unit is a septic tank with some bells and whistles; there is no monitoring, there is no control, and with the distributed wastewater to meet the definition of the Florida Legislature that they established there actually has to be monthly reporting of the water quality that is leaving the unit that is made to Florida Department of Environment Protection (FDEP) each month; just like the County’s own utility has to make its monthly reporting to FDEP, so does the units that are distributed wastewater; he will turn it over to Jeff Littlejohn who is actually a professional engineer; and maybe he can add to that.
Jeff Littlejohn commented great question, he thinks Mr. Vinyard covered it very well for an attorney; Mr. Vineyard gives him credit for being an engineer, but honestly, that is a pretty good answer; and he thinks the primary benefit of having that continuous monitoring and then monthly testing is the County gets reasonable assurance that it is actually getting the nutrients out of the system that it is paying for if one is contributing taxpayer funds to a program like this, or if a homeowner is paying for this type of technology or if a new developer is paying for this type of technology, the State, and in this case the County would have the assurance that the wastewater is actually being treated to that high standard because it is verified every month.
Commissioner Pritchett stated Chair Altman just came off of the State of Florida; and she asked if you guys ever did anything to make it so that homeowners had to get inspections done on their septic.
Chair Altman pointed out the State passed a law way back about 10 or 12 years ago, Senator Lee Constantine's Bill, that required that; there was a revolt against it because of the fees, the cost of getting inspectors out there; he forgets if it was annual or bi-annual; even in between inspections, one really does not know what is going on; and it was repealed the next year, it did not get very far.
Commissioner Pritchett repeated they did not get very far on that one.
Chair Altman noted this is far superior to that; he might say, too, he has been incredibly impressed with the team that On-site has put together; Mr. Vineyard, former director of the FDEP, and Mr. Littlejohn is very knowledgeable engineer; they have operators of a pretty respectable sewer treatment facilities; that said, the County is not committing to them, it is forcing them to go out and selectively bid, so the County will send the word out and see; and it will come back to the Board so it can review the proposals.
Commissioner Pritchett stated it sounds good; and she asked if there are any downfalls to this that would just be any kind of hesitation with it the Board would have to overcome.
Mr. Littlejohn replied honestly, he was trying to think of what would be a downside; it is a more complex piece of technology than a conventional septic tank, certainly; it is a more complex piece of technology than an advanced septic tank; it is a mini wastewater treatment plant; there are multiple pumps, a blower, a computer, and there are things that fail; the good news is it is continuously monitored by a professional, so when failure occur, they know about it immediately; they do not rely on the homeowner to tell them there is an alarm going off, or their toilet will not flush, it is remotely controlled and monitored so that a technician can be dispatched to fix it; he thinks if there is a downside, maybe they are sending technicians to people’s neighborhoods and homes, and knocking on the door asking if they can fix his or her wastewater plan in their backyard, maybe a little bit more visitation; and whether the Board thinks that as a downside or upside, it is assurance that the equipment is working.
Chair Altman noted before it backs up in ones living room.
Mr. Vinyard commented to further answer Commissioner Pritchett’s question, one of the larger or bigger near-term advantages is, as the Board heard in its presentation about its new advanced wastewater treatment plant; it is $150 million; it is going to take multiple years to bring that system online; this is something that the County could do in 30 days in an individual home; and the opinion that the Lagoon cannot wait, this is immediate technology that could be deployed at a far lower cost.
Commissioner Pritchett mentioned it is very interesting to her; up in District 1, there is a lot of property right now; actually, someone called her, they were going to buy a place on Burkholm Road but were told not a good time to buy because a house cannot be built as a septic system cannot be put in; there are kind of a lot of stuck areas in District 1 right now; it is something the County is trying to figure out what to do to help; she wishes this whole thing would just go away; but she cannot control judges. She stated whoever brought this up, it is interesting, thanks.
Chair Altman pointed out when he heard about this, he got excited; he has been worried, sitting on the Value Adjustment Board, it is a time bomb; if this Bear Warrior case is not overturned, there is an economic time waiting to go off when all of these properties, thousands of acres, suddenly are undevelopable; it never ceases to amaze him the power of a Federal judge; he has asked the County Attorney to explain it to him, but it is scary to think how one individual can just shut down a county; the County Attorney has tried to educate him, but it is amazing; one thinks of all of the rule making, studies, land use planning, and all of the things done to properly plan for growth or septic services, and to think there is a single individual who can just decide it is going to be shut down; and it has gone before an 11-judge panel in Atlanta that the County is waiting for.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, explained it went before the 11th Circuit Court in April for oral argument, and they have not, unless it happened today or yesterday about issue of opinion; and he is sure he would have heard by now had they . . .
Chair Altman stated if there is a downside, and he does not think there is any, but if there were one, it is new technology, so it is not proven; the County is a pioneer; he thinks it is proven technology but the implementation has not been done, and the County wants to be cutting edge; second, it may be an advantage; it can be a little bit of a disadvantage but it might turn out to be a big advantage; it does a better job than traditional septic tanks in getting the phosphorus out; but the County has not completely fixed the phosphorus challenge, which is also tough on the Lagoon; and there is research being done that this solution may even be able to address the problem with phosphorus, which would be huge in terms of the Lagoon and quality, so the County is hopeful with that.
Mr. Littlejohn expressed his appreciation to Chair Altman for bringing up phosphorus; he stated the City of Apopka, which also runs a distributed wastewater treatment system program similar to the one that has been talked about; they received an innovative technology grant from FDEP; they are partnering with the City of Apopka to study a phosphorus removal modification to their existing technology that would strip the phosphorus out; they are very optimistic; they have done a lot of testing; he believes they are going to pass with flying colors and then they will have a unit for nitrogen only; and they will have a unit for nitrogen and phosphorus.
Chair Altman stated this is great.
Commissioner Feltner asked who is going to own the units in the future, it is put in the ground, but who owns it.
Mr. Vinyard responded it would be the County; the way the State is set up the permitting process, they all have to be commonly owned and operated; in this case, it would be the County; if this was a new development, theoretically could be a Homeowners Association (HOA) or a Community Development District (CDD) that could own it; but in these instances, it would be the County; he and Mr. Littlejohn have a background at FDEP; and what they have found in their time there, specifically with the BATUs, the snazzy septic tanks, homeowners make terrible wastewater plant operators; and that is why it has to be put into the hands of government or an HOA, a more responsible entity.
Commissioner Feltner stated they talked about a technician having to come in the future; and he asked when that happens, if the County Utility Services is going to pay for that.
Mr. Vinyard responded they can offer that as a turnkey thing; of course, it will be in the RFP if that worked out; but they have people that do that.
Commissioner Feltner inquired if in 10 years from now, the unit has been in the ground, there is some kind of an issue, the technician comes out and services the unit, if that is going to be Brevard County Utility Services that is going to get the bill. He stated the County owns it, so it will get the bill.
Mr. Littlejohn responded that is a great question; the structure of that has made the most sense with their other municipal partners, so Lake County, Santa Rosa County, and City of Apopka, is that the County owns and operates the equipment as it does with a lift station, collection system, or central plant; the homeowners that receive service from that utility-owned wastewater infrastructure receive a sewer bill; the sewer bill that the homeowners pays for receiving public sewer service covers the ongoing cost of operation, repair, replacement, testing, compliance, and everything; their role, as a contract provider in all of those scenarios, is they service all of the equipment in accordance with their contract with their municipal partner, in accordance with all of their regulatory requirements from FDEP; they do not charge the County something additional if something breaks, as it is just part of a standard service agreement, fixed-fee model; and they are going to cover everything for that fixed-fee. He noted again, they are going to describe all of this if they have an opportunity to respond to this RFP; he reiterated the homeowner does not have to pay anything other than the monthly sewer bill as if they were attached to . . .
Chair Altman interjected by saying if he may make a point, those are good questions, he has more; this is all by choice, it is something the consumer chooses; it is not being inflicted onto anybody this system; it is a landowner, property owner, or homeowner that chooses to have this system; what is interesting is it really is very cost competitive with some of the state-of-the-art, or the non-state-of-the-art onsite treatment systems; what really motivated him with this, and he is obviously getting calls from people who cannot even use their land in some of these land, two or three-unit acre lots, but he purchased a home in Lake Poinsett that had one of these so called new systems, and was horrified; he was horrified how poorly the system worked, how often it broke, how the pumps would quit running, and not stop running and dumping the sewage out; he always thought these new systems were so great, and they are not, and not knowing if they were working or not working; and thirdly, how unresponsive and expensive these private septic tank companies are in maintaining the systems, the lack of ability for them to even service, and the money one spends, it is kind of the wild west there and simply not working. He reiterated again that this is an exciting alternative, and the County will see how it works, as it is a test; and he guesses it is an innovative system that may have great dividends.
Commissioner Feltner commented there was a very good meeting in his office and it was explained if one is considering building a new home and one has this Federal issue that may be impeding them; this is a way for one to be able to build his or her home and put this system in; and he asked to put it in the ground, the homeowner is going to pay that bill.
Mr. Vinyard replied the way they have typically done it is they would pay the local government a monthly fee just like homeowners on the County sewer system; and homeowners would pay the monthly fee and then they would contract with the County to operate, maintain, and service it.
Commissioner Feltner asked what the upfront costs would be, he is just going to use round numbers; and one of these things cost $30,000 on a property.
Mr. Vinyard stated less than that.
Commissioner Feltner stated $20,000 that goes in the ground; and he asked who gets the bill for that, the County.
Mr. Vinyard responded in the case of a new construction that would be borne by the homeowner, but that would be in exchange . . . you know, they are going to build a house; it is like the countertops are borne by the homeowner, so is the wastewater system in that case; and in other areas where they have done septic to sewer, FDEP is actually funding grants for homeowners to convert septic systems over to distributed wastewater treatment systems.
Commissioner Feltner mentioned he understands, so on a new construction, the homeowner, just like they would a septic tank, they have that expense; then, they will get a sewer bill from the County for the maintenance of it; and when there is maintenance and potentially they come out, they bill the County, the County charges the homeowner a sewer fee.
Mr. Vinyard responded it is built into the bulk fee that they would charge the County, so it is not like . . . unless the homeowner, for example, damaged . . . you know, it is like if one’s kid takes a baseball bat to his or her electric meter, that is not covered in a person’s normal electric fees; but if a pump goes out, or something like that, the typical things that go wrong would be covered in the monthly fee that the homeowner pays to the County.
Commissioner Feltner explained when they came to meet with him, a lot of technical issues were discussed; and he is sure there will be more moving along.
Commissioner Pritchett advised she is interested in it, she is working out all of the financial details; she asked if any of this would qualify for some Lagoon funds since it is an upgrade on what the County is doing with advanced septic, because it did that for a long time with advanced septic; and she stated that might be something that would help the homeowners because that would be hard to digest $20,000 for this.
Mr. Vinyard stated they think it would; Commissioner Pritchett is talking about the County’s specific Lagoon tax that Brevard County has; it is certainly something that FDEP is funding today; and his suspicion is, and he will refer to the County Attorney, is the language that allows the County to spend the money would cover this.
Commissioner Pritchett stated either that or the County has to give Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director, a lot more money so he can build a whole another system in North Brevard.
James Morris commented he and his wife live in Port St. John, and they are actually the other side of this; they bought a property about five years ago in Merritt Island, they are both firefighters; his wife was working as a nurse during COVID as well; they bought their property, working on trying to build, and they had some hurdles; they got set back by the interest rates going up; when they finally found the right builder, everything lined up for them; and then their builder told them, “hey, you can’t get a permit.” He went on to say as the Board can imagine, this is supposed to be their forever home; he started digging, he started calling them, calling around trying to see if they are really in this moratorium; a corner of their lot on Merritt Island falls right inside that line; again setbacks; but in those talks, he again spoke with FDEP, and they actually suggested that as well. He stated he is thankful he is here to thank the Board for looking at this; without it, he cannot build their family home; as the Board knows, without it, he cannot build their family home that they want to live forever in cannot happen unless that Federal judge overturns it; obviously, he thinks they would all be frustrated; he is here to say thanks for working with anybody who is willing to find solutions, and for trying to help them; even without the moratorium after learning about the wastewater treatment systems, he and his wife talked about it, and they would like to do it either way; the fact that it is monitored, he knows it is working; they are reporting levels to the FDEP; on top of that, his sewer bill, he thinks when he talked to them, he thinks they said it was probably about 50 bucks; and it covers all of the maintenance and any repairs included. He noted to him it is a win/win, especially with Amendment 3 coming down, the talks of all of the budgets, wastewater needs, the new facility being $150 million is costing the County nothing, but giving them the ability to build their home.
Richard Heffelfinger asked why the District 5, Chair, is raising this and bringing this as something for the residents consider; he stated this sure sounds SOIRLish, unless the objection is to beat the septic moratorium or whatever about that; he asked if this system qualifies that the County can put this in and beat that right now; he advised if it does not, then the Board needs to find that out first because this is going to cost if he understands it right, let him see if he does; these guys are here and they can tell him; he has a standard septic system and he loves it and it works; he asked if the Board wants to know why he knows it works, because the crap does not back up in his shower, and when it does not, crap backs up in his shower; and he noted he has it pumped, it is inspected. He went on to say his system is working, the leach field is . . . now, does it meet current Code requirements, no, because if he had to, he should be so many more inches above, the resting groundwater; it needs to be bigger, he has been told because he thought about modifying it and immediately decided not to because they said the County has to come up to Code; he knows it is not the best, but he has an acre; as long as his density does not get too high, the Earth can handle a certain amount; they get density higher, it cannot, so the County needs more efficient systems; Save Our Indian River Lagoon (SOIRL) is spending a lot of its money to install these; he thinks, on this chart that was attached to this, they are installing the enhanced nitrogen reduction septic performance-based treatment system; he asked if that is true, and what the County knows; and he stated that is what they are installing. He advised the County and SOIRL is paying for some of that; he realizes that is probably only if one is in the SOIRL high-risk area to try to because the County’s leaching would go into the groundwater close to the river, get the river, so they want to do that; this system sounds like it is superior in performance; this would be a good thing for SOIRL to be researching saying to get the max hit for the money; the company is a little lower; he assumes that on this chart they are the private package treatment plants, no; and he asked what numbers are theirs, or he does not know what they are.
Commissioner Pritchett pointed out he should not be talking to the applicant.
Chair Altman asked Mr. Heffelfinger to address his comments to the Board, instead of trying to . . .
Mr. Heffelfinger interjected by saying he just wanted to make sure that he is comparing apples to oranges.
Chair Altman asked Mr. Heffelfinger to give his questions to the public, and if . . .
Mr. Heffelfinger stated they are actually not quite as good as enhanced nitrogen for removing nitrogen; he asked if that was true; and he stated he does not understand . . . so the homeowner has a leach field, and he asked if these guys just put sensors on it.
Chair Altman stated he thinks these are wonderful questions and if the County proceeds with the RFP, there will be a lot of data and time to answer them; Mr. Heffelfinger asked a question, why District 5; he stated he is looking at a map of the five Districts of the County, because all of the Commissioners represent the County; he has massive areas of land in his District; actually it affects all five Commissioners; it is a huge impact on a County like Brevard; what really inspired him, he has three wonderful kids and two wonderful grandkids that are at the age of trying to buy homes and start their lives, and he has friends who call him; their friends are calling them and him saying, “Your Dad’s a County Commissioner, I just invested my life savings. My wife and I just got married. We want to have a family. We literally can’t even build now on a lot that we just bought”, and he stated just as the testimony that was just had from Mr. Morris; and it is tragic, stealing people’s dreams. He noted that was really the motivation to him; secondly, having a home that has one of these so-called new systems, seeing how poorly they operate, and how bad the industry is and how difficult it is; thirdly, the impacts on the Lagoon; there are a lot of reasons that he personally got involved in; did a lot of due diligence, and a lot of time was spent before bringing it to this level; and he reiterated again that he was excited about it.
Mr. Heffelfinger stated he would think that would be the reason, his logic is perfect; that would be a reason why SOIRL should be looking at this as an alternative to what they are paying for now; if this is that much better, and it is not going to . . . because the SOIRL system fails, and nobody knows, until the pump backs up and poops in one’s shower like he gets; but one does not know the leach field . . . well, say there is a crack in the tank; and that is kind of the worst think he guesses, so this is monitored and he likes that. He reiterated if there are costs, he thinks SOIRL should bear the cost to do the research the Chair is asking for; find out if better sewer capacity can be high capacity septic; they cannot go to sewer because there is no sewer; and if it does not meet the moratorium, then he does not know why the Board would even pursue it unless it gets it out from under the moratorium. He mentioned he does not know why the advancements do not currently today gets the County out from the moratorium.
Chair Altman stated he thinks the testimony was approved, and he feels the same, he is interested in this; and regardless of the moratorium, it is a better system.
Mr. Heffelfinger noted he would like to make sure SOIRL pays for it if it can because that needs to be maximized.
Commissioner Adkinson advised she is going to support this Agenda Item, not because she knows anything about this, because the applicants did not come to her, so she has no idea; she has a whole list of questions, she thinks that if staff can educate the Board by answering all of the questions that he or she has; if the other Commissioners can be patient, she is going to list what her questions are; she asked how many companies do this; why does the County have to hold the FDEP permit; why the vendor cannot do it, because it seems like the County would be left holding the bag if something goes wrong; is the Board holding the bag when something goes wrong or when the company goes bust; she stated she understands they have a proprietary platform; this is all above her head, so she does not understand it; but she needs to know what that means for the County if the company it picks does go bust. She asked if a pilot program could be done in just a small area rather than just eventually saying this is going to be done Countywide; could a small area study be done; and she mentioned those are her questions that hopefully will get answered when the Board gets the report back.
Commissioner Pritchett stated those are really good questions; she asked piggybacking off of that, what the typical cost for repairs would be if it breaks, so the County knows it is charging enough to cover all of those incidentals; she stated she is very interested in it; but she does not have any of those dollar numbers as far as the costs and what the County is looking at coming back in, because the County cannot put it on the backs of other taxpayers.
Chair Altman explained a lot of those questions are going to be better answered, this is not committing the County to anything; he thinks those are good points and good questions; he is looking forward to hearing some of those as well; he appreciates the questions by the Commission because it makes him realize he or she has a grasp of just how significant this is; this could be epic and could have a huge impact, he thinks, in a positive way; but those are the questions that make him realize how big this is and how important; he reiterated he is looking forward to having some of those questions answers; he has taken a personal interest in this because he is interested in the Lagoon, the technology, and Brevard has had many years of challenges; and he has had personal decades of fighting the septic issue.
Jim Liesenfelt, County Manager, advised the County Attorney, Central Services Director, and himself was double-checking; Commissioner Adkinson mentioned they had not visited; staff met with the onsite folks twice; once this RFP is voted for, the County is in a cone of silence; Onsite cannot visit the Commissioners; they cannot be visiting staff either; and he just wanted to make sure of that because this is a little different than a normal RFP.
Chair Altman stated once the RFP is released, then once it is . . . how about when the Board receives it prior to the . . . at what point can the Board and staff start meeting with them.
Commissioner Pritchett stated typically, when the County has done RFPs, it already kind of knows the cost to the County; she asked if staff has any of that already; she stated she is getting a little . . . she is thinking like an accountant, she cannot help it right now.
Ms. Wall explained what she envisions is a component of this RFP will be price, because staff does not know the price of this system yet; and there will be five or six components, and one of them will be price.
Commissioner Pritchett inquired if the County needs to know the cost of maintenance and those types of things; and she asked if staff has those.
Ms. Wall replied that would also be part of the RFP; staff will get all of the data; and it will be the cost of the capital, the cost to maintain, and she reiterated those costs will be part of the RFP.
The Board authorized Purchasing Services permission to advertise a Request for Proposals (RFP) to solicit competitive sealed proposals to furnish septic to individual distributed wastewater treatment systems within Brevard County, Florida; approved a Selection and Negotiating Committee comprised of Virginia Barker, Natural Resources Management Director, Marc Bernath, Public Works Director, and Edward Fontanin, Utility Services Director to review the received proposals; and directed staff to bring the highest-ranked proposal, along with negotiated contract, back to the Board for its consideration.
body: Brevard County Board of County Commissioners
title: Permission to Advertise Re: Request for Proposal (RFP) to Solicit Competitive Sealed Proposals to Furnish Septic to Individual Distributed Wastewater Treatment Systems within Brevard County, Florida

Richard Heffelfinger stated he really wanted to address this during Item E.1., but there were no comments; E.1. is very nice because it says there is a challenge coming if the County does a referendum and it loses a large portion of real estate tax; that challenge already exists today; they know that because the County did an impact study; the County has multiple things that are in serious backlog of potential that even an impact fee is not going to save lives; the impact fees was one possible solution to try to address those issues; Fire Rescue, over the next 10 years, has gotten an $87 million cost estimate that is not covered as far as he knows, the way that the impact study was done, $19 million for correction facilities, Libraries has $18 million, Solid Waste does not have any because that has been handled in other ways, and the worst one is transportation; and it is $3,561,000 worth of backlog that he knows the County has now. He went on to say wait if these things get passed; he asked what happens to that; it has been many years as this backlog did not happen overnight; he thinks there is already a solution that was provided by the Board during its budget review or the Budget Workshop process; the Board did get some possible solutions that were inside that workshop and it just has not executed any of them, they have been showed to the Board. He stated how about County and regional transportation system discretionary sales surtax, that could give additional revenue $25 to $100 million; United States government infrastructure discretionary sales surtax, $37 million; public services taxes ninth cent fuel tax; fuel taxes was talked about; nobody wanted to take that up; and he reiterated those have been presented, yet the Board has not taken the bite yet. He mentioned the Board is going to have to take the bite, especially if this happens; it needs to take the bite now because the residents already has a serious backlog over the next 10 years; it is going to have to do something; and not doing anything is no longer an option. He stated he does not even care if this does not pass this referendum that says the County pulls $51 million off of it in the first year, he thinks is what was in the numbers; $51 million is nothing compared to the current backlog that it has, and the impact fee showed it had; staff has actually provided answers, as they were in some of those workshops; but nobody grabbed those and said, they need to get out of this; and it only gets worst every year the Board does not do anything. He remarked there were a lot of potential things in that . . . and the solution is the County just needs to take those; instead of saying no, it does not want to do that, he or she is going to have to say it is going to have to do that, or the deficit continues to grow, it will grow even faster if this passes; the action has been on the table for years, the Board just has to start taking it, and those solutions are already on the table, it just has to enact them, make a motion to make staff put forward . . . it has to tell them to do that; and that is the only way it is going to get it done.
Chair Altman advised that Mr. Heffelfinger is 100 percent right; he really appreciates what he just said; it is not an easy thing to say, but it is true; it takes courage, commitment, and vision for the future; and he reiterated he agrees with him.

Commissioner Pritchett interjected by saying to go ahead.

Commissioner Pritchett inquired if she needs to do anything different with the motion such as restate the items in the BDP.
Morris Richardson, County Attorney, noted it would be helpful at this point.
Chair Altman advised before the motion, he has a question; he noticed when up in this part of the County on U.S. 1, there is a delineation line off of U.S. 1 where it limits the depth of commercial that is allowed; this large back parcel seems to exceed that line and encroached commercial deeper into the neighborhoods; and he asked if that was considered as he knows it was in the staff’s comments.
Mr. Prasad replied yes, that is why the Small Scale amendment is needed because the NC currently is that strip closer to U.S.1, the RES 2 designation is on the eastern portion; that is why the land use designation change is being requested from NC and RES 2 to CC, or at least the back part; and that RES 2 portion is what is being requested to change to CC.
Chair Altman commented that makes sense.
An audience member asked for more explanation.
Mr. Prasad explained in addition to zoning, the Comprehensive Plan sets out Future Land Use designations and only compatible zonings can go in those land use designations; in this case the current Land Use designations are Neighborhood Commercial (NC) and RES 2, which is a Residential Land Use classification; and one of the things the applicant is requesting is a change to Community Commercial (CC) on the entire parcel which is compatible with BU-1.
Commissioner Feltner asked for clarification that if Item H.4. does not prevail, what it would do with H.5.
Mr. Prasad advised Item H.5. could not be approved without Item H.4. being approved as the Land Use designation must be changed to consider BU-1.
Commissioner Feltner commented if they do not get that then they have to reconsider what zoning potential change they would do in the future.
Mr. Prasad responded affirmatively.
An audience member interjected by saying the Board is basically telling them, the people who live there, that they do not have a say in this.
Chair Altman explained that is why the Board has Public Comment.
The audience member commented it does not sound like the Board is listening though.
Chair Altman advised the Board has not made a decision yet.
The audience member shouted the Board is destroying their property and asked why.
Chair Altman advised everyone had five minutes to speak and the Board has spent 30 minutes discussing; it is not that the Board is not listening…
The audience member stated he got more than five and he is able to speak again.
Chair Altman explained he is the applicant.
The audience member noted they do not live there and this is their homes, there is a school right there.
Chair Altman asked the audience member to give the Board an opportunity to deliberate on this.
The audience member noted it does not sound like Commissioner Pritchett is doing too good of a job.
Chair Altman asked again to allow the Board to deliberate a little bit on this.
An audience member stated and they have to walk out of here living with this Board’s decision.
Another audience member shouted they live there and this is their lives.
More outbursts from the audience.
Chair Altman called for a break.
The Board recessed at 5:54 p.m. and reconvened at 6:01 p.m.
Chair Altman commented the Board was in deliberation; it has procedures that it must follow; there are five minutes per speaker, 15 minutes for the applicant; there is some time left in the applicant’s presentation; and he would like to maybe answer some of the questions.
Mr. Ferraro stated they have just had some good discussion with people that are going to put a house right here; this is on the east side; they can actually go ahead and increase that buffer to 100 feet; and he does not think it is going to impact the development based on the size of the building that is going to be there, if that helps the Board.
Attorney Richardson asked if the Board heard Commissioner Goodson’s vote.
Commissioner Goodson advised he is for it.
There being no further comments or objections, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 2026-13, amending Article III, Chapter 62, of the Code of Ordinances of Brevard County, entitled “The 1988 Comprehensive Plan”’ setting forth the fifth Small Scale Plan amendment of 2026, 26S.05 to the Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan; amending Section 62-501 entitled Contents of the Plan; specifically amending Section 62—501, Part XVI(E), the Future Land Use Appendix; and provisions which require amendment to maintain internal consistency with these amendments; providing legal status; providing a severability clause; and providing an effective date.

action_text: The Board of County Commissioners acts as a Quasi Judicial body when it hears request for rezoning and Conditional Use Permits. Applicants must provide competent substantial evidence establishing facts, or expert witness opinion testimony showing that the request meets the Zoning Code and Comprehensive Plan criteria. Opponents must also testify as to facts, or provide expert testimony; whether they like, or dislike, a request is not competent evidence. The Board must then decide whether the evidence demonstrates consistency and compatibility with the Comprehensive Plan and the existing rules in the Zoning Ordinance, property adjacent to the property rezoned, and the actual development of the surrounding area. The Board cannot consider speculation, non expert opinion testimony, or poll the audience by asking those in favor or opposed to stand up or raise their hands. If a Commissioner has had communications regarding a rezoning or Conditional Use Permit request before the Board, Commissioner must disclose the subject of the communication and the identity of the person, group, or entity, with whom the communication took place before the Board takes action on the request. Each applicant is allowed a total of 15 minutes to present their request unless the time is extended by a majority vote of the Board. The applicant may reserve any portion of the 15 minutes for rebuttal. Other speakers are allowed five minutes to speak. Speakers may not pass their time to someone else in order to give that person more time to speak.
